batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::05 Functional Programming::04 Streams

cards.front: What happens to a stream pipeline that has no terminal operation?
cards.back: Nothing runs - a stream processes no data without a terminal operation
cards.extra: Intermediate operations only build up the pipeline. Terminal operations such as count(), forEach(), max() or collect() are what pull the elements through it.
cards.example:
java.util.stream.Stream pipeline = java.util.stream.Stream.of("a", "b")
    .peek(x -> System.out.println("visited " + x)).map(String::toUpperCase);
System.out.println("built, nothing visited");

cards.front: Why is reduce() recommended only as a last resort among terminal operations?
cards.back: You must prove the operator is associative and check for an identity first
cards.extra: Getting either wrong silently produces wrong results, especially in parallel streams. sum(), min(), max(), count() and the collectors cover almost every real reduction.
cards.example:
java.util.List xs = java.util.List.of(1, 2, 3);
int sum = xs.parallelStream().reduce(0, Integer::sum);
String bad = xs.stream().map(String::valueOf).reduce("", (a, b) -> b + a);
System.out.println(sum + " " + bad);

cards.front: Which line returns the number of elements a stream processes?
cards.extra: count() exists on every stream interface, object and primitive specializations alike, and returns a long rather than an int.
cards.example:
java.util.stream.Stream stream = java.util.stream.Stream.of("a", "b", "c");
long n = stream.count();
System.out.println(n);

cards.front: What is the return type of Stream.count()?
cards.extra: A stream can process more than Integer.MAX_VALUE elements, for example after a flatMap() multiplies the element count, so the API supports counts beyond int range.
cards.example:
long n = java.util.stream.Stream.of("a", "b").count();
System.out.println(n);

cards.front: Why does Collectors.counting() exist when streams already have count()?
cards.back: So counting can be a downstream collector of another collector such as groupingBy
cards.extra: A plain terminal method cannot be composed. Once counting is itself a Collector it can be plugged in to replace the List values a grouping produces.
cards.example:
java.util.Map counts = java.util.stream.Stream.of("a", "bb", "cc")
    .collect(java.util.stream.Collectors.groupingBy(s -> s.length(), java.util.stream.Collectors.counting()));
System.out.println(counts);

cards.front: Why is stream.forEach(System.out::println) an acceptable use of a side effect?
cards.back: Printing is the intended effect; a consumer that does nothing has no purpose
cards.extra: The problem is not side effects per se but side effects on shared state outside the stream, such as mutating a captured list.
cards.example:
java.util.stream.Stream.of("hello", "world").parallel().forEach(System.out::println);
java.util.stream.Stream.of("hello", "world").parallel().forEach(x -> {});

cards.front: What breaks when you fill a list with stream.forEach(result::add)?
cards.back: Capturing an external mutable list makes the result unsafe: ArrayList cannot take concurrent writes from a parallel stream
cards.extra: result::add captures a variable outside the stream's scope, and an ArrayList cannot safely take concurrent writes from the threads of a parallel stream.
cards.example:
java.util.List result = new java.util.ArrayList<>();
java.util.stream.Stream.of("a", "b", "c").parallel().forEach(result::add);
System.out.println(result.size());

cards.front: Which collector stores elements in a list with no side effect from your code?
cards.extra: The Collector API owns the accumulation and the merging of per-thread partial results, so the same code works sequentially or in parallel.
cards.example:
java.util.List result = java.util.stream.Stream.of("a", "b")
    .collect(java.util.stream.Collectors.toList());
System.out.println(result);

cards.front: What does stream.toList() return since Java SE 16?
cards.extra: It may also be faster than Collectors.toList(), which accumulates into an ArrayList and seals it afterwards, because the JDK can size the backing array up front.
cards.example:
java.util.List list = java.util.stream.Stream.of("a", "b").toList();
try { list.add("c"); } catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) { System.out.println("unmodifiable"); }

cards.front: Which collector lets you choose the concrete collection class?
cards.extra: The supplier creates the empty container, so () -> new ArrayList<>(10_000) pre-sizes the array and avoids repeated grow-and-copy cycles.
cards.example:
java.util.LinkedHashSet set = java.util.stream.Stream.of("b", "a", "b")
    .collect(java.util.stream.Collectors.toCollection(java.util.LinkedHashSet::new));
System.out.println(set);

cards.front: Which factory method returns an unmodifiable set from a stream?
cards.extra: Its sibling toUnmodifiableList() seals a List the same way. Any attempt to modify the returned collection throws UnsupportedOperationException.
cards.example:
java.util.Set set = java.util.stream.Stream.of("a", "b", "a")
    .collect(java.util.stream.Collectors.toUnmodifiableSet());
try { set.add("c"); } catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) { System.out.println("unmodifiable"); }

cards.front: Which toArray() overload preserves the stream's element type?
cards.extra: The no-arg toArray() returns Object[], losing the component type even when the stream was declared as Stream<String>.
cards.example:
String[] a = java.util.stream.Stream.of("a", "b").toArray(String[]::new);
System.out.println(a.getClass().getSimpleName() + " " + a.length);

cards.front: Which two arguments does Stream.max() on a stream of objects require?
cards.back: Only a Comparator, since elements can be of any type
cards.extra: The numeric specializations IntStream, LongStream and DoubleStream know how to compare numbers and take no comparator, returning OptionalInt and friends.
cards.example:
java.util.List xs = java.util.List.of("pear", "apple");
String max = xs.stream().max(String::compareTo).orElseThrow();
System.out.println(max);

cards.front: Why do max(), min() and average() return optional objects?
cards.back: None has an identity element, so an empty stream has no result
cards.extra: Calling get() on an empty Optional throws NoSuchElementException, so use orElse() or orElseThrow() when the stream might produce no elements.
cards.example:
java.util.Optional max = java.util.stream.Stream.empty().max(Integer::compareTo);
java.util.Optional min = java.util.stream.Stream.empty().min(Integer::compareTo);
java.util.OptionalDouble avg = java.util.stream.IntStream.empty().average();
System.out.println(max.isPresent() + " " + min.isPresent() + " " + avg.isPresent());

cards.front: On an unordered stream, what does findFirst() return?
cards.back: Any element - first is undefined, so it behaves like findAny()
cards.extra: Order matters only for ordered sources such as a List. With Set.of() the traversal order is randomized, so findFirst() returns a random element.
cards.example:
String first = java.util.stream.Stream.of("x", "y").unordered().findFirst().orElseThrow();
String any = java.util.stream.Stream.of("x", "y").unordered().findAny().orElseThrow();
System.out.println(first + " " + any);

cards.front: Why prefer findAny() over findFirst() on a parallel stream?
cards.back: Tracking the first element forces extra coordination, a cost findAny does not pay
cards.extra: findFirst() must guarantee ordering even across worker threads. If any matching element will do, findAny() lets threads return the first they happen to find.
cards.example:
String any = java.util.stream.Stream.of("a", "b", "c").parallel().findAny().orElseThrow();
String first = java.util.stream.Stream.of("a", "b", "c").parallel().findFirst().orElseThrow();
System.out.println(any + " " + first);

cards.front: What does anyMatch(pred) return for an empty stream?
cards.extra: No element was found to match, so the answer is negative. The predicate is never invoked because there is nothing to test it against.
cards.example:
boolean matched = java.util.stream.Stream.empty().anyMatch(s -> s.length() > 0);
System.out.println(matched);

cards.front: What does allMatch(pred) return for an empty stream?
cards.extra: Vacuously true: no element violates the predicate. noneMatch() also returns true for an empty stream for the mirror reason.
cards.example:
boolean all = java.util.stream.Stream.empty().allMatch(s -> s.isEmpty());
System.out.println(all);

cards.front: Which single terminal operation is not short-circuiting among findAny, anyMatch and count?
cards.extra: It must process every element to produce a total. findFirst(), findAny(), anyMatch(), allMatch() and noneMatch() can stop once the answer is settled.
cards.example:
java.util.stream.Stream s = java.util.stream.Stream.of("a", "bb", "ccc")
    .peek(x -> System.out.println("seen " + x));
long n = s.count();
System.out.println(n);

cards.front: When can anyMatch(pred) stop before consuming the whole stream?
cards.back: As soon as one element matches and it can return true
cards.extra: To return false it must see every element first. That asymmetry is why a returning true is short-circuiting but a returning false is not.
cards.example:
java.util.stream.Stream s = java.util.stream.Stream.of("a", "bb", "ccc")
    .peek(x -> System.out.println("seen " + x));
boolean hit = s.anyMatch(x -> x.length() == 2);
System.out.println(hit);

cards.front: When does findFirst() have to process every element?
cards.back: Only when the stream is empty and it must return an empty Optional
cards.extra: findFirst() short-circuits the moment it has an element. Proving the absence of any element is the one case that requires the whole pipeline to run.
cards.example:
java.util.Optional first = java.util.stream.Stream.of("a", "bb")
    .peek(x -> System.out.println("seen " + x)).findFirst();
System.out.println(first.orElse("empty"));
java.util.Optional empty = java.util.stream.Stream.empty().findFirst();
System.out.println(empty.isPresent());

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::05 Functional Programming::04 Streams

cards.front: Which Stream.collect() overload is missing from the numeric streams?
cards.extra: Numeric streams keep only the three-argument collect(supplier, accumulator, combiner). To use Collectors with them, box() the stream first.
cards.example:
int sum = java.util.stream.IntStream.of(1, 2, 3).sum();
java.util.List boxed = java.util.stream.IntStream.of(1, 2, 3).boxed()
    .collect(java.util.stream.Collectors.toList());
System.out.println(sum + " " + boxed);

cards.front: Why should code not depend on the concrete class returned by Collectors.toList()?
cards.back: The exact List implementation is not part of the specification
cards.extra: The JDK is free to change it between releases. Declare the variable as List and use toCollection() when you need a specific implementation.
cards.example:
java.util.List list = java.util.stream.Stream.of("a", "b")
    .collect(java.util.stream.Collectors.toList());
System.out.println(list.getClass().getName());

cards.front: Which collector joins a stream of strings with a separator, prefix and suffix?
cards.extra: It also handles empty and single-element streams correctly, producing just prefix+suffix and prefix+element+suffix respectively.
cards.example:
String text = java.util.stream.Stream.of("a", "b")
    .collect(java.util.stream.Collectors.joining(", ", "[", "]"));
System.out.println(text);

cards.front: When should you use String.join() instead of Collectors.joining()?
cards.back: When the data is already a collection or only a few elements - no stream needed
cards.extra: joining() requires building a pipeline and pays the stream overhead. String.join() and StringJoiner do the same work without it.
cards.example:
java.util.List parts = java.util.List.of("a", "b", "c");
String joined = String.join(", ", parts);
System.out.println(joined);

cards.front: What map type does Collectors.partitioningBy(predicate) produce?
cards.extra: Every element goes under the true or false key depending on the predicate, so only two keys can ever exist, both always present.
cards.example:
java.util.Map> parts = java.util.stream.Stream.of("a", "bb")
    .collect(java.util.stream.Collectors.partitioningBy(s -> s.length() == 1));
System.out.println(parts);

cards.front: What is the function passed to Collectors.groupingBy() called?
cards.extra: It maps each element to a key. Elements sharing a key are gathered into a list, which yields Map<K, List<T>> when no downstream collector is given.
cards.example:
java.util.function.Function classifier = String::length;
java.util.Map> groups = java.util.stream.Stream.of("a", "bb")
    .collect(java.util.stream.Collectors.groupingBy(classifier));
System.out.println(groups);

cards.front: What is the only restriction on the classifier passed to groupingBy()?
cards.extra: Any other function is allowed, and several elements may map to the same key, since groupingBy collects them into a List under that key.
cards.example:
java.util.List xs = java.util.List.of("a", "b");
try { xs.stream().collect(java.util.stream.Collectors.groupingBy(s -> null)); }
catch (NullPointerException e) { System.out.println("null key rejected"); }

cards.front: What happens when Collectors.toMap() sees two elements producing the same key?
cards.extra: toMap builds one entry per element and cannot choose a survivor. Supply a BinaryOperator merge function as the third argument to resolve collisions.
cards.example:
java.util.List xs = java.util.List.of("a", "a");
try { xs.stream().collect(java.util.stream.Collectors.toMap(x -> x, x -> 1)); }
catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println(e.getClass().getSimpleName()); }

cards.front: Which three arguments does the merge-aware Collectors.toMap() take?
cards.back: Key mapper, value mapper and a BinaryOperator merge function
cards.extra: The merge function receives the old and the new value when a duplicate key appears and returns what should be stored instead.
cards.example:
java.util.List words = java.util.List.of("a", "b", "a");
java.util.Map counts = words.stream().collect(java.util.stream.Collectors.toMap(
    w -> w, w -> 1, Integer::sum));
System.out.println(counts);

cards.front: Which minor collector variant of toMap() writes into a concurrent map?
cards.extra: It lets a parallel stream merge partial results without locking; the exact map class returned is still not guaranteed.
cards.example:
java.util.Map m = java.util.stream.Stream.of("a", "b", "a").parallel()
    .collect(java.util.stream.Collectors.toConcurrentMap(x -> x, x -> 1, Integer::sum));
System.out.println(m);

cards.front: How do you stream the entries of a Map?
cards.extra: Map has no stream() method. Key only is map.keySet().stream(), and values only is map.values().stream().
cards.example:
java.util.Map map = java.util.Map.of("a", 1, "b", 2);
map.entrySet().stream().forEach(e -> System.out.println(e.getKey() + "=" + e.getValue()));

cards.front: Which factory method builds a Comparator over Map.Entry values?
cards.extra: It only works when the values are Comparable. comparingByKey() provides the analogous comparator over keys.
cards.example:
java.util.Map m = java.util.Map.of("a", 2, "b", 1);
java.util.Map.Entry best = m.entrySet().stream()
    .max(java.util.Map.Entry.comparingByValue()).orElseThrow();
System.out.println(best.getKey());

cards.front: Which two collectors convert a value into a different type than a plain group?
cards.extra: Both must be given a downstream collector as their second argument, so they exist only inside another collector such as groupingBy.
cards.example:
java.util.List xs = java.util.List.of("a", "bb", "ccc");
java.util.List lens = xs.stream().collect(java.util.stream.Collectors.mapping(
    String::length, java.util.stream.Collectors.toList()));
java.util.List longOnes = xs.stream().collect(java.util.stream.Collectors.filtering(
    s -> s.length() > 1, java.util.stream.Collectors.toList()));
System.out.println(lens + " " + longOnes);

cards.front: What extra argument do the mapping, filtering and flatMapping collectors require?
cards.extra: They model intermediate operations, which have no terminating step of their own. The downstream collector supplies the terminal half of the behavior.
cards.example:
java.util.List xs = java.util.List.of("1", "2");
java.util.List nums = xs.stream().collect(java.util.stream.Collectors.mapping(
    Integer::parseInt, java.util.stream.Collectors.toList()));
System.out.println(nums);

cards.front: What type does Collectors.averagingInt(fn) produce?
cards.extra: Unlike IntStream.average(), which returns an OptionalDouble, the averaging collectors never return an optional; an empty stream averages to 0.0.
cards.example:
Double avg = java.util.stream.Stream.of("a", "bb")
    .collect(java.util.stream.Collectors.averagingInt(String::length));
System.out.println(avg);

cards.front: What does Collectors.maxBy(cmp) return when the stream is empty?
cards.extra: minBy() behaves identically. As with Stream.max(), the result is optional because no identity element exists.
cards.example:
java.util.Optional max = java.util.stream.Stream.empty()
    .collect(java.util.stream.Collectors.maxBy(String::compareTo));
System.out.println(max.isEmpty());

cards.front: What does a partitioning collector's map always contain, even for an empty stream?
cards.extra: The two booleans are fixed, so the result type is Map<Boolean, List<T>>. In contrast, groupingBy only creates keys that actually occur.
cards.example:
java.util.Map> parts = java.util.stream.Stream.empty()
    .collect(java.util.stream.Collectors.partitioningBy(s -> s.isEmpty()));
System.out.println(parts.keySet());

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::06 Concurrency::06 Virtual Threads in Practice

cards.front: When did virtual threads become a final (non-preview) feature of Java?
cards.extra: They were introduced as a preview by JEP 425 in Java 19, previewed again in Java 20, and finalized in Java 21.
cards.example:
// Java 21: virtual threads are final, not a preview feature (no --enable-preview)
Thread t = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> System.out.println("running"));
try { t.join(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
System.out.println(t.isVirtual()); // true

cards.front: What happens to a virtual thread when it blocks?
cards.back: It is unmounted and its carrier thread runs another virtual thread
cards.extra: Many virtual threads share a small pool of platform carrier threads. Unmounting frees the carrier while the blocked task waits, so blocking no longer wastes an OS thread.
cards.example:
// A blocked virtual thread unmounts; its carrier can run another virtual thread
Thread v = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> java.util.concurrent.locks.LockSupport.park());
Thread other = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> System.out.println("another one ran"));
java.util.concurrent.locks.LockSupport.unpark(v);

cards.front: Which factory method runs each task in its own virtual thread?
cards.extra: It returns an ExecutorService. It is also the only creation route that supports Callables and therefore result-bearing tasks.
cards.example:
try (var ex = java.util.concurrent.Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
  ex.submit(() -> System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().isVirtual())); // task 1
  ex.submit(() -> System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().isVirtual())); // task 2
} // close waits for both

cards.front: Which virtual-thread creation route supports result-bearing Callable tasks?
cards.extra: Thread.Builder, Thread.ofVirtual().start() and startVirtualThread() all take a Runnable, so they cannot return a value.
cards.example:
try (var ex = java.util.concurrent.Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
  java.util.concurrent.Future f = ex.submit(() -> "result"); // Callable
  System.out.println(f.get());
} catch (Exception e) { throw new RuntimeException(e); }

cards.front: What thread group do virtual threads belong to?
cards.extra: There is no API to create a virtual thread in a different group, and calling setPriority() or setDaemon() on one has no effect.
cards.example:
Thread a = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> {});
Thread b = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> {});
System.out.println(a.getThreadGroup() == b.getThreadGroup()); // true: one shared group

cards.front: Are virtual threads daemon or non-daemon?
cards.extra: Because they are daemons they never keep the JVM alive. Both properties are fixed and cannot be changed with setters.
cards.example:
Thread v = Thread.ofVirtual().unstarted(() -> {});
System.out.println(v.isDaemon() + " " + (v.getPriority() == Thread.NORM_PRIORITY)); // true true

cards.front: Does Thread.getAllStackTraces() include virtual threads?
cards.extra: Virtual threads are not enumerated by that legacy method. There is also no way to find which carrier platform thread a given virtual thread runs on.
cards.example:
Thread v = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> System.out.println("running"));
boolean listed = Thread.getAllStackTraces().containsKey(v);
System.out.println(listed); // false: only platform threads are listed

cards.front: Which method tells whether a Thread instance is virtual?
cards.extra: Virtual threads are ordinary Thread instances, so this boolean is the only way to distinguish them. Cancellation still uses Thread.interrupt().
cards.example:
Thread platform = Thread.currentThread();
Thread virtual = Thread.ofVirtual().unstarted(() -> {});
System.out.println(platform.isVirtual() + " " + virtual.isVirtual()); // false true

cards.front: Why should you not pool virtual threads?
cards.back: A pool caps concurrency and defeats cheap creation; pooled virtual threads still run on platform carrier threads
cards.extra: Virtual threads are cheap to create, so make one per task. Use semaphores or per-resource limits for rate limiting instead.
cards.example:
// Pooling virtual threads gives back the platform-thread scheduling cost they remove
var perTask = java.util.concurrent.Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(); // one thread per task
var fixed = java.util.concurrent.Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4); // reused platform threads
perTask.submit(() -> "task"); fixed.submit(() -> "task");

cards.front: How do you limit concurrent access to a scarce resource when using virtual threads?
cards.back: Use a Semaphore per resource rather than shrinking a thread pool
cards.extra: Semaphore.acquire() blocks when the permit count runs out, which is cheap on a virtual thread. Each limited resource gets its own protection.
cards.example:
java.util.concurrent.Semaphore slots = new java.util.concurrent.Semaphore(2);
try (var exec = java.util.concurrent.Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    exec.submit(() -> { slots.acquireUninterruptibly(); try { System.out.println("using"); } finally { slots.release(); } });
}

cards.front: How many carrier threads does the virtual thread scheduler use by default?
cards.back: As many as there are CPU cores
cards.extra: Tune it with the jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism VM option. jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.maxPoolSize caps the carrier pool when compensation kicks in.
cards.example:
int cores = Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors();
System.out.println(cores); // default carrier count: one per available CPU core
Thread t = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> System.out.println("scheduled"));
try { t.join(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }

cards.front: In JDK 21 to 23, which two situations pin a virtual thread to its carrier?
cards.back: Running a synchronized method or block, or a native or foreign function call
cards.extra: A pinned thread cannot be unmounted while it blocks. Replacing synchronized with ReentrantLock removes the first cause, and JDK 24 fixes it in the JVM.
cards.example:
// JDK 21-23 pinning: synchronized blocks/methods and native or foreign calls
Thread v = Thread.ofVirtual().unstarted(() -> {
  synchronized (String.class) { java.util.concurrent.locks.LockSupport.park(); } // pinned
});
v.start(); // a native/foreign call while blocked pins the same way

cards.front: Why is pinning dangerous when the pinned thread blocks?
cards.back: The carrier stays blocked and, in JDK 21, no extra carrier is started to replace it
cards.extra: With all carriers stuck, other virtual threads are left unscheduled. Pinning in purely in-memory synchronized code is harmless, since nothing blocks.
cards.example:
Object lock = new Object();
Thread t = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> { synchronized (lock) {
    java.util.concurrent.locks.LockSupport.parkNanos(10_000_000L); } });
System.out.println(t.isVirtual());

cards.front: Which VM flag prints a stack trace when a pinned virtual thread blocks?
cards.extra: You get only one warning per pinning location. Alternatively record with JFR and look for VirtualThreadPinned and VirtualThreadSubmitFailed events.
cards.example:
// Run with -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full: a pinned thread that blocks logs a stack trace
Thread t = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> {
  synchronized (String.class) { java.util.concurrent.locks.LockSupport.park(); }
});
System.out.println(t.getName()); // the flag prints where the carrier was pinned

cards.front: Which VM flag traces virtual threads that mutate thread-local variables?
cards.extra: Since virtual threads vastly outnumber pooled platform threads, thread locals multiply with them. The trace shows where per-thread state is being created.
cards.example:
// -Djdk.traceVirtualThreadLocals traces virtual threads that change thread-local variables
ThreadLocal local = new ThreadLocal<>();
Thread t = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> local.set("value"));
System.out.println(t.isVirtual());

cards.front: For which workload are virtual threads not useful?
cards.extra: Their win comes from unmounting blocked threads, which never happens for compute-bound work. Use parallel streams or fork-join for those instead.
cards.example:
// CPU-bound work rarely blocks, so unmounting gives no scheduling gain
long n = java.util.stream.LongStream.range(0, 1_000_000L).filter(x -> x % 2 == 0).count();
Thread v = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> System.out.println(n)); // no benefit here

cards.front: Why is the non-final Thread.getId() deprecated in favour of threadId()?
cards.back: A subclass could override getId() and return a value that is not the real id
cards.extra: Callers who need the real identity must use the final threadId(). getId() has been deprecated since Java 19 alongside static thread factories.
cards.example:
class Ex {
  static class Fake extends Thread { public long getId() { return -1; } } // not final: overridable
  static void m() { Thread t = new Fake();
    System.out.println(t.getId() + " vs " + t.threadId()); // -1 vs the real id
  }
}

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.front: Which class represents a contiguous region of memory in the Foreign Function and Memory API?
cards.extra: It is backed either on-heap (a heap segment) or off-heap (a native segment). Off-heap segments are the ones used for native calls.
cards.example:
import java.lang.foreign.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
try (Arena arena = Arena.ofConfined()) {
MemorySegment segment = arena.allocate(8);
System.out.println(segment.byteSize());
} } }

cards.front: Why must arguments to a C function live in off-heap memory?
cards.back: The GC may move or free heap memory, and native code cannot follow that
cards.extra: Native code needs a stable address. Off-heap memory is outside the GC's reach, so you also decide exactly when it is deallocated.
cards.example:
import java.lang.foreign.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
try (Arena arena = Arena.ofConfined()) {
MemorySegment arg = arena.allocateFrom("hi"); // stable off-heap address for native code
System.out.println(arg.address() != 0);
} } }

cards.front: What governs the lifetime of a native memory segment?
cards.back: The arena used to allocate it - its scope decides when the memory is freed
cards.extra: A segment is accessible while its scope is alive. Closing the arena invalidates every segment allocated from it at once.
cards.example:
Arena arena = Arena.ofConfined();
MemorySegment seg = arena.allocate(64);
arena.close();
// the arena's scope ended, so seg is no longer accessible

cards.front: Which arena restricts its segments to the thread that created it?
cards.extra: It has an owner thread, usually the creator. Closing it from another thread, or accessing its segments there, fails.
cards.example:
import java.lang.foreign.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
Arena confined = Arena.ofConfined(); MemorySegment seg = confined.allocate(4);
System.out.println(confined.scope().isAlive()); // owner thread only
confined.close();
} }

cards.front: Which arena lets any thread access and close its segments, with close being atomic?
cards.extra: It has no owner thread, so multiple threads can read and write its segments concurrently. Slice-based parallel processing relies on it.
cards.example:
import java.lang.foreign.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
Arena shared = Arena.ofShared(); MemorySegment seg = shared.allocate(8);
Thread.ofPlatform().start(() -> seg.set(ValueLayout.JAVA_INT, 0, 7)).join();
shared.close(); // atomic close waits for all accessors
} }

cards.front: What happens when you call close() on Arena.global() or on an automatic arena?
cards.extra: The global arena's memory is never deallocated, and the automatic arena's memory is managed by the garbage collector, so neither can be closed by hand.
cards.example:
import java.lang.foreign.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
try { Arena.global().close(); } catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) { System.out.println("global"); }
try { Arena.ofAuto().close(); } catch (UnsupportedOperationException e) { System.out.println("auto"); }
} }

cards.front: What does SegmentAllocator.allocateFrom(String) store in the segment?
cards.extra: It allocates, converts and copies in one call, which is exactly what a C function expecting a char* needs.
cards.example:
import java.lang.foreign.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
SegmentAllocator allocator = Arena.ofConfined();
MemorySegment text = allocator.allocateFrom("hi");
System.out.println(text.byteSize());
} }

cards.front: What is a ValueLayout used for when accessing a memory segment?
cards.back: It encodes the size, byte order, alignment and Java type of the value
cards.extra: Every get or set takes one. ValueLayout.JAVA_BYTE, for instance, is one byte, aligned to 1 and uses the hardware's native byte order.
cards.example:
import java.lang.foreign.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
ValueLayout layout = ValueLayout.JAVA_INT.withOrder(java.nio.ByteOrder.nativeOrder());
System.out.println(layout.byteSize() + " " + layout.alignment() + " " + layout.carrier());
} }

cards.front: What happens if you access a segment whose arena has been closed?
cards.extra: The scope is no longer alive so the segment is invalid. Allocating the arena in a try-with-resources block makes this state impossible to reach by accident.
cards.example:
import java.lang.foreign.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
Arena arena = Arena.ofConfined(); MemorySegment seg = arena.allocate(4); arena.close();
try { seg.get(ValueLayout.JAVA_INT, 0L); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println(e); }
} }

cards.front: Which method builds a StructLayout describing a C struct?
cards.extra: Pass one value layout per field in declaration order, for example a JAVA_INT for the numerator and one for the denominator of a C fraction.
cards.example:
import java.lang.foreign.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
MemoryLayout layout = MemoryLayout.structLayout(ValueLayout.JAVA_INT.withName("x"), ValueLayout.JAVA_DOUBLE.withName("y"));
System.out.println(layout.byteSize());
} }

cards.front: What is a VarHandle in the context of memory segments?
cards.back: A strongly typed reference to read and write a field at a known offset
cards.extra: Obtained from a group layout, it lets you set or get a named field of a struct without recomputing offsets by hand.
cards.example:
import java.lang.foreign.*;
import java.lang.invoke.VarHandle;
class Ex { static void m() {
Arena arena = Arena.ofConfined();
MemorySegment segment = arena.allocate(MemoryLayout.structLayout(ValueLayout.JAVA_INT.withName("numerator")));
StructLayout layout = MemoryLayout.structLayout(ValueLayout.JAVA_INT.withName("numerator"));
VarHandle numerator = layout.varHandle(PathElement.groupElement("numerator"));
numerator.set(segment, 0L, 7);
System.out.println(numerator.get(segment, 0L));
} }

cards.front: Which call retrieves the layout of field numerator inside a struct layout?
cards.extra: The result is turned into a VarHandle for a given layout, memory segment and offset, then reused to access every instance of the struct.
cards.example:
import java.lang.foreign.*;
import java.util.Optional;
class Ex { static void m() {
StructLayout layout = MemoryLayout.structLayout(ValueLayout.JAVA_INT.withName("numerator"));
Optional member = layout.member(PathElement.groupElement("numerator"));
System.out.println(member.orElseThrow());
} }

cards.front: Which three arguments does VarHandle.set() take for a struct field?
cards.back: The memory segment, the base offset and the value
cards.extra: The offset lets the handle address an element inside an array of structs in a single call, without computing an address manually.
cards.example:
import java.lang.foreign.*; import java.lang.invoke.VarHandle;
class Ex { static void m() {
StructLayout layout = MemoryLayout.structLayout(ValueLayout.JAVA_INT.withName("n")); VarHandle n = layout.varHandle(PathElement.groupElement("n"));
MemorySegment seg = Arena.ofAuto().allocate(layout);
n.set(seg, 0L, 7); // segment, base offset, value
} }

cards.front: What does SegmentAllocator.slicingAllocator(segment) return?
cards.back: An allocator that hands out consecutive slices of an existing segment
cards.extra: Each allocation carves the next chunk right after the previous one, which is how an array of structs is laid out in memory.
cards.example:
Arena arena = Arena.ofConfined();
MemorySegment backing = arena.allocate(64);
SegmentAllocator slicing = SegmentAllocator.slicingAllocator(backing);
MemorySegment first = slicing.allocate(8);
MemorySegment second = slicing.allocate(8);
System.out.println(first.address() < second.address());

cards.front: Which method returns a slice of any size from any position inside a segment?
cards.extra: The offset and size must stay within the original segment's spatial bounds; a slice that would overrun them is rejected.
cards.example:
import java.lang.foreign.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
MemorySegment seg = Arena.ofConfined().allocate(16);
MemorySegment slice = seg.asSlice(4L, 8L);
System.out.println(slice.byteSize());
} }

cards.front: Which arena do you need when threads process the slices of one segment in parallel?
cards.extra: Concurrent access requires the segment to be reachable from every thread, and only a shared arena allows that.
cards.example:
java.lang.foreign.Arena shared = java.lang.foreign.Arena.ofShared();
java.lang.foreign.MemorySegment segment = shared.allocate(1024);
// threads can process slices of the same segment in parallel

cards.front: What does jextract do?
cards.back: Parses C header files and generates Java bindings that use the FFM API
cards.extra: You then program against a Java model of the native library instead of writing downcall handles and layouts by hand.
cards.example:
jextract -d gen -t generated mylib.h
# generates Java bindings with FFM API calls for the C declarations in mylib.h

cards.front: In which JDK release did the Foreign Function and Memory API become final?
cards.extra: It had been developed as part of Project Panama, with repeated previews, before that finalization.
cards.example:
import java.lang.foreign.*;
// JDK 22 made the Foreign Function and Memory API final (no --enable-preview)
Arena arena = Arena.ofAuto();
MemorySegment seg = arena.allocate(8);
System.out.println(seg.byteSize());

cards.front: Which jextract option sets the package of the generated classes?
cards.extra: Without it the classes land in the unnamed package. jextract also creates the package directories under the directory given by --output.
cards.example:
jextract -t com.example.windows Windows.h
# -t / --target-package sets the generated classes' package

cards.front: Which jextract option links a shared library that the generated header class loads?
cards.extra: A name like -l GL means a library name; a leading colon like -l :libGL.so.1 means a file path.
cards.example:
jextract -l GL -d gen gl.h
jextract --library GL -d gen gl.h
# the generated header class loads the shared library named by -l / --library

cards.front: What is the default header class name jextract derives from a header file foo.h?
cards.extra: Override it with --header-class-name. That option is mandatory when you pass more than one header file to a single run.
cards.example:
jextract -d gen foo.h
# generated header class: gen.foo_h

cards.front: Why use --dump-includes before filtering a huge header?
cards.back: It lists every symbol so you can then keep only the ones you want in an argfile
cards.extra: Windows.h is an extreme case. Edit the dump, remove unneeded lines, and pass the file back with the @argfile syntax.
cards.example:
jextract --dump-includes includes.txt Windows.h
# edit includes.txt to keep only the symbols you want
jextract @includes.txt Windows.h

cards.front: What happens if a filter removes a declaration that an included struct still needs?
cards.back: jextract reports the missing dependency and generates nothing
cards.extra: You must then re-include the dependency. Filtering is not silently Lenient: an incomplete symbol set aborts the whole run.
cards.example:
jextract -I . --filter 'foo_.*' --output gen foo.h
# foo_Use needs struct Bar, which the filter removed: no bindings generated

cards.front: Which two wildcard imports give access to everything jextract generated for freeglut.h into package org.freeglut?
cards.extra: The static import brings functions, constants and macros as static members; the plain import brings the struct and typedef classes.
cards.example:
import static org.freeglut.freeglut_h.*;
import org.freeglut.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
System.out.println("jextract-generated types and constants are visible");
} }

cards.front: Which VM flag enables jextract's native call tracing?
cards.extra: With it, the parameters passed to each native call are printed on standard output, which makes debugging argument mistakes much quicker.
cards.example:
java -Djextract.trace.downcalls=true -cp gen Main
# jextract-generated downcalls print their arguments at runtime

cards.front: Which tool generates a C interface for a Rust library so jextract can consume it?
cards.extra: For C++ the equivalent route is to consume the library's extern "C" declarations. Either way jextract works through a C surface.
cards.example:
cbindgen --lang c --crate mylib --output mylib.h
jextract -I . -d gen mylib.h

cards.front: What is a downcall method handle?
cards.back: A MethodHandle that points to a native function and can be invoked from Java
cards.extra: You get it from the linker by combining the function's address with a FunctionDescriptor describing its signature.
cards.example:
import java.lang.foreign.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
Linker linker = Linker.nativeLinker();
java.lang.invoke.MethodHandle abs = linker.downcallHandle(linker.defaultLookup().find("abs").orElseThrow(), FunctionDescriptor.of(ValueLayout.JAVA_INT, ValueLayout.JAVA_INT));
System.out.println(abs);
} }

cards.front: Which class describes the argument and return layouts of a native function?
cards.extra: Its first layout is the return type and the rest are the parameters. Each layout maps to the Java type used when invoking the handle.
cards.example:
java.lang.foreign.FunctionDescriptor fd =
    java.lang.foreign.FunctionDescriptor.of(java.lang.foreign.ValueLayout.JAVA_INT,
        java.lang.foreign.ValueLayout.ADDRESS);
// return layout first, then parameter layouts

cards.front: Which value layout models a C pointer argument or return value?
cards.extra: A char* is also commonly described as a sequence layout of JAVA_BYTE, to express a NUL-terminated byte string.
cards.example:
java.lang.foreign.ValueLayout pointer = java.lang.foreign.ValueLayout.ADDRESS;
System.out.println(pointer); // a C pointer argument or return value

cards.front: Why is a native function signature description platform specific?
cards.back: Widths vary: size_t is JAVA_LONG on 64-bit, JAVA_INT on 32-bit
cards.extra: Check the layouts your platform actually uses with Linker.canonicalLayouts() rather than hardcoding widths.
cards.example:
import java.lang.foreign.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
System.out.println(Linker.canonicalLayouts().get("size_t"));
// 64-bit: JAVA_LONG; 32-bit: JAVA_INT
} }

cards.front: Which lookup finds symbols in a user-specified library using the standard loader search?
cards.extra: It is the right choice for functions in the C standard library, such as strdup, so you need no OS-specific file name.
cards.example:
import java.lang.foreign.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
SymbolLookup lookup = Linker.defaultLookup();
MemorySegment abs = lookup.find("abs").orElseThrow();
System.out.println(abs);
} }

cards.front: Which lookup searches libraries already loaded by System.loadLibrary()?
cards.extra: libraryLookup(name, arena) instead loads a named library on demand and ties its lifetime to the given arena.
cards.example:
import java.lang.foreign.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
System.loadLibrary("mylib");
SymbolLookup lookup = SymbolLookup.loaderLookup();
System.out.println(lookup.find("my_function").isPresent());
} }

cards.front: Which method builds a downcall handle from an address and a descriptor?
cards.extra: Different orders exist across JDK versions; the address still uniquely identifies the symbol and the descriptor supplies its types.
cards.example:
import java.lang.foreign.*;
import java.lang.invoke.MethodHandle;
class Ex { static void m() {
Linker linker = Linker.nativeLinker();
MemorySegment address = linker.defaultLookup().find("abs").orElseThrow();
MethodHandle handle = linker.downcallHandle(address,
FunctionDescriptor.of(ValueLayout.JAVA_INT, ValueLayout.JAVA_INT));
} }

cards.front: Why must the type descriptor at an invokeExact() call match the handle exactly?
cards.back: invokeExact rejects any mismatch with the handle's type descriptor
cards.extra: Use invoke() instead when you want the arguments coerced. For FFM handles the C signature and the Java call must line up precisely.
cards.example:
import java.lang.invoke.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Throwable {
MethodHandle h = MethodHandles.lookup().findStatic(Math.class, "abs", MethodType.methodType(int.class, int.class));
int r = (int) h.invokeExact(-5); // descriptor must match exactly, or it fails
} }

cards.front: Which two composite layouts model C struct and union types?
cards.extra: GroupLayout is their common supertype, sufficient when a descriptor only needs to say a parameter or return is a group.
cards.example:
java.lang.foreign.GroupLayout struct = java.lang.foreign.StructLayout.createLayout(
    java.lang.foreign.ValueLayout.JAVA_INT, java.lang.foreign.ValueLayout.JAVA_INT);
java.lang.foreign.GroupLayout union = java.lang.foreign.UnionLayout.createLayout(
    java.lang.foreign.ValueLayout.JAVA_INT, java.lang.foreign.ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG);
// both are GroupLayouts

cards.front: What does the FFM API return to represent a pointer whose target size it cannot know?
cards.extra: That is what a pointer from malloc, from an upcall, or read out of a segment looks like. It carries the address but no bounds.
cards.example:
import java.lang.foreign.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
MemorySegment unknownSize = MemorySegment.NULL;
System.out.println(unknownSize.byteSize());
} }

cards.front: What happens if you read the content of a zero-length memory segment?
cards.extra: The JVM cannot validate access to a region of unknown size, so it refuses. The segment is still useful for passing back to native code.
cards.example:
import java.lang.foreign.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
MemorySegment zero = MemorySegment.NULL;
try { zero.get(ValueLayout.JAVA_BYTE, 0); }
catch (IndexOutOfBoundsException e) { System.out.println(e.getClass().getSimpleName()); }
} }

cards.front: Which method turns a zero-length segment into one with real bounds and a lifetime?
cards.extra: Give the byte count, the arena that takes ownership, and an action to run on close such as calling C's free().
cards.example:
import java.lang.foreign.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
MemorySegment zero = MemorySegment.NULL; try (Arena arena = Arena.ofConfined()) {
MemorySegment sized = zero.reinterpret(8, arena, ignored -> {});
System.out.println(sized.byteSize());
} } }

cards.front: Which linker option captures errno after a native call?
cards.extra: It snapshots the thread-local state immediately after the downcall. Read it from a MemorySegment of the right layout to see what C set.
cards.example:
import java.lang.foreign.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
Linker link = Linker.nativeLinker();
var state = Arena.global().allocate(Linker.Option.captureStateLayout().byteSize());
var h = link.downcallHandle(link.defaultLookup().find("sqrt").orElseThrow(), FunctionDescriptor.of(ValueLayout.JAVA_DOUBLE, ValueLayout.JAVA_DOUBLE), Linker.Option.captureCallState("errno"));
} }

cards.front: Which VM option enables native calls without restricted-method warnings?
cards.extra: Multiple modules take a comma-separated list. An executable JAR can set the manifest attribute Enable-Native-Access instead.
cards.example:
# Without this, restricted FFM calls print warnings
java --enable-native-access=com.example app.Main
java --enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED -cp . Main

cards.front: Why is SymbolLookup.libraryLookup() a restricted method?
cards.back: Loading a library executes native code, for instance through dlopen hooks
cards.extra: The JVM cannot inspect what library initialization does, so the operation requires explicit opt-in from the application author.
cards.example:
SymbolLookup lookup = SymbolLookup.libraryLookup("mylib.so", Arena.global());
MemorySegment f = lookup.find("my_function").orElseThrow();
// restricted: loading a library executes native code, e.g. dlopen hooks

cards.front: Why is MemorySegment.reinterpret(long) restricted?
cards.back: An overestimated size can make later access read outside the real region
cards.extra: That can crash the JVM or silently corrupt memory, so resizing a segment's view needs an explicit native-access grant.
cards.example:
import java.lang.foreign.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
MemorySegment seg = Arena.ofConfined().allocate(8);
MemorySegment bigger = seg.reinterpret(1024L);
System.out.println(bigger.byteSize()); // overestimated size can read outside the real region
} }

cards.front: Why is Linker.downcallHandle() restricted?
cards.back: The linker cannot verify that the FunctionDescriptor matches the real C function
cards.extra: A wrong descriptor misinterprets argument and return widths, which is undefined behavior rather than a predictable exception.
cards.example:
Linker linker = Linker.nativeLinker();
MemorySegment abs = linker.defaultLookup().find("abs").orElseThrow();
// restricted: the linker cannot verify the descriptor matches the real C function
var handle = linker.downcallHandle(abs, FunctionDescriptor.of(ValueLayout.JAVA_INT, ValueLayout.JAVA_INT));

cards.front: In a manifest's Enable-Native-Access attribute, what values are allowed?
cards.back: Only ALL-UNNAMED - a module name is rejected
cards.extra: A JAR cannot name a module, so the manifest route grants native access to everything on the class path.
cards.example:
# META-INF/MANIFEST.MF inside the executable JAR
Enable-Native-Access: ALL-UNNAMED
# Enable-Native-Access: com.example.M  is rejected

cards.front: What is an upcall in the FFM API?
cards.back: A call from native code back into a Java method, passed as a function pointer
cards.extra: The classic use is qsort, which needs a comparison callback. Java supplies its code as a pointer the native library can invoke.
cards.example:
import java.lang.foreign.*; import java.lang.invoke.*;
class Ex { static int compare(MemorySegment a, MemorySegment b) { return 0; } static void m() throws Throwable {
MethodHandle h = MethodHandles.lookup().findStatic(Ex.class, "compare", MethodType.methodType(int.class, MemorySegment.class, MemorySegment.class));
MemorySegment ptr = Linker.nativeLinker().upcallStub(h, FunctionDescriptor.of(ValueLayout.JAVA_INT, ValueLayout.ADDRESS, ValueLayout.ADDRESS), Arena.ofAuto());
System.out.println(ptr.address() != 0); // native code can call ptr
} }

cards.front: What is an upcall stub?
cards.back: A native function pointer created by the linker that invokes a Java MethodHandle
cards.extra: You build it with Linker.upcallStub(handle, descriptor, arena) and hand it to the native function as a callback argument.
cards.example:
import java.lang.foreign.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
java.lang.invoke.MethodHandle cb = java.lang.invoke.MethodHandles.lookup().findStatic(Ex.class, "log", java.lang.invoke.MethodType.methodType(void.class));
MemorySegment stub = Linker.nativeLinker().upcallStub(cb, FunctionDescriptor.ofVoid(), Arena.ofConfined());
} static void log() {} }

cards.front: Which method finds an upcall stub's linkable function pointer for a Java method handle?
cards.extra: It needs the handle, the descriptor matching the C signature, and an arena that owns the stub's lifetime.
cards.example:
import java.lang.foreign.*;
import java.lang.invoke.*;
class Ex { static void cb() { } static void m() throws Throwable {
MethodHandle h = MethodHandles.lookup().findStatic(Ex.class, "cb", MethodType.methodType(void.class));
MemorySegment ptr = Linker.nativeLinker().upcallStub(h, FunctionDescriptor.ofVoid(), Arena.ofAuto());
} }

cards.front: Why are the comparator's parameters of type MemorySegment in a Java implementation for qsort?
cards.back: Native code passes pointers, so each element arrives as a segment, not as an int
cards.extra: You unwrap them with get(ValueLayout.JAVA_INT, offset) using the byte offset given by qsort, then return a negative, zero or positive int.
cards.example:
import java.lang.foreign.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
// native qsort passes element pointers, so comparator arguments are segments
java.util.Comparator<MemorySegment> cmp = (a, b) -> Integer.compare(a.get(ValueLayout.JAVA_INT, 0), b.get(ValueLayout.JAVA_INT, 0));
System.out.println(cmp);
} }

cards.front: Which arena is appropriate for an upcall stub whose lifetime follows the GC?
cards.extra: The garbage collector decides when to free the stub, which suits a callback used for the duration of a single native call.
cards.example:
import java.lang.foreign.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
Arena arena = Arena.ofAuto();
java.lang.invoke.MethodHandle h = java.lang.invoke.MethodHandles.lookup().findStatic(Ex.class, "cb", java.lang.invoke.MethodType.methodType(void.class));
MemorySegment stub = Linker.nativeLinker().upcallStub(h, FunctionDescriptor.ofVoid(), arena);
} static void cb() {} }

cards.front: How do you get a MethodHandle for a static Java method with MethodHandles.Lookup?
cards.extra: It takes the declaring class, the method name and a MethodType describing the return type plus every parameter type.
cards.example:
import java.lang.invoke.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Throwable {
MethodHandles.Lookup lookup = MethodHandles.lookup();
MethodHandle abs = lookup.findStatic(Math.class, "abs", MethodType.methodType(int.class, int.class));
System.out.println((int) abs.invokeExact(-5));
} }

cards.front: Which method lists the root directories of a file system?
cards.extra: It returns an Iterable, so an enhanced for loop can walk every root. On Windows that is every drive letter; on UNIX usually just /.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
for (Path root : FileSystems.getDefault().getRootDirectories()) System.out.println(root);
} }

cards.front: Which method creates a single directory and fails if a parent is missing?
cards.extra: It takes optional FileAttributes to set at creation. Use createDirectories() when intermediate parents may not exist.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
Files.createDirectory(Path.of("parent/child")); // fails if parent is missing
Files.createDirectories(Path.of("parent/child")); // creates parents as needed
} }

cards.front: Which method creates a directory together with any missing parents?
cards.extra: It works top-down: foo, then bar, then test. If a step fails, some of the parents may already have been created.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
Path p = Files.createDirectories(Path.of("a/b/c"));
System.out.println(Files.isDirectory(p));
} }

cards.front: Which file-system exception type signals that a directory was not empty?
cards.extra: Files.delete() throws it for a non-empty directory, as does a copy with REPLACE_EXISTING onto one.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
Path dir = Files.createTempDirectory("t");
Files.writeString(dir.resolve("f"), "x");
try { Files.delete(dir); } catch (DirectoryNotEmptyException e) { System.out.println("not empty"); }
} }

cards.front: How do you create a temporary directory in the default temporary location?
cards.extra: The overload taking a Path puts it in a directory you choose instead. The name format after the prefix is platform specific.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
Path dir = Files.createTempDirectory("logs"); // default temporary location
} }

cards.front: Which class is the legacy way to model a file and should no longer be used?
cards.extra: Path with the Files factory methods replaced it in Java SE 7 with more features and better performance on large directories.
cards.example:
import java.io.File;
import java.nio.file.Path;
class Ex { static void m() {
File legacy = new File("a.txt"); // legacy file model
Path modern = Path.of("a.txt"); // preferred since Java SE 7
} }

cards.front: Does creating a File instance touch the file system?
cards.back: No - it is only an abstract pathname, and every query is explicit
cards.extra: Constructing File or Path never creates anything. Existence, permissions and content all require a separate call.
cards.example:
import java.io.File;
class Ex { static void m() {
File f = new File("no-such-file.txt");
System.out.println(f.exists()); // an explicit query, not construction
} }

cards.front: What does File.getCanonicalPath() return that getAbsolutePath() does not?
cards.back: An absolute unique path: ./.. removed, links resolved
cards.extra: Only the canonical form is guaranteed unique, which is why it is the one you compare when two paths may name the same file.
cards.example:
import java.io.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
File f = new File("./sub/../a.txt");
System.out.println(f.getAbsolutePath());
System.out.println(f.getCanonicalPath());
} }

cards.front: Which File method gives just the last name element of the path?
cards.extra: getParent() gives the directory containing it, and getPath() gives the whole abstract pathname as text.
cards.example:
import java.io.File;
class Ex { static void m() {
File f = new File("a/b/c.txt");
System.out.println(f.getName());
} }

cards.front: Since which Java release does the Path interface exist?
cards.extra: It is the primary entry point of java.nio.file. Legacy code can migrate with File.toPath().
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*; import java.io.File;
class Ex { static void m() {
Path p = Path.of("a.txt"); // java.nio.file.Path since Java SE 7
System.out.println(p + " " + new File("a.txt").toPath());
} }

cards.front: Which method converts a legacy File to a Path?
cards.extra: Path.toFile() goes the other way. The migration is preferred over rewriting I/O code wholesale.
cards.example:
import java.io.File;
import java.nio.file.Path;
class Ex { static void m() {
Path p = new File("a.txt").toPath();
System.out.println(p);
} }

cards.front: Is a Path portable across operating systems?
cards.back: No - it uses the syntax of the platform it was created on
cards.extra: A Solaris Path and a Windows Path never compare equal even when they name the same relative location with the same directory tree.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
Path p = Path.of("a", "b");
System.out.println(p.getFileSystem().getSeparator() + " " + p);
} }

cards.front: Which File method returns true only if the file already exists?
cards.back: exists() — createNewFile() returns false when the file is already there, but it also creates a file when it is not
cards.extra: It returns false rather than overwriting, and throws IOException only if creation failed for another reason.
cards.example:
import java.io.File;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
File f = new File("new.txt");
f.createNewFile();
System.out.println(f.exists() + " " + f.createNewFile());
} }

cards.front: Which method retrieves the default file system?
cards.extra: Note the plural on the factory class FileSystems and the singular on the returned FileSystem.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
FileSystem fs = FileSystems.getDefault();
System.out.println(fs.getSeparator() + " " + fs.isReadOnly());
} }

cards.front: What path separator does a POSIX file system use, and what does Windows use?
cards.extra: Read it from FileSystem.getSeparator() instead of hardcoding, since other file systems may use other delimiters.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
System.out.println(FileSystems.getDefault().getSeparator());
System.out.println("POSIX: / ; Windows: \\");
} }

cards.front: What does a file store represent?
cards.back: The underlying storage device behind a file system, such as a mounted volume
cards.extra: On UNIX each mounted file system is a store; on Windows each volume is one. List them with getFileStores().
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
for (FileStore store : FileSystems.getDefault().getFileStores()) System.out.println(store.name());
} }

cards.front: How do you build a Path directly from a FileSystem?
cards.extra: Paths.get() and Path.of() are convenience wrappers around exactly this call, which is why all three are interchangeable.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
Path p = FileSystems.getDefault().getPath("u", "joe", "foo.log");
System.out.println(p);
} }

cards.front: Which file system does a new Path bind to when none is supplied?
cards.extra: Every Path belongs to a file system; omitting one simply selects FileSystems.getDefault(), the operating system's own file system.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
Path p = Path.of("u", "joe", "foo.log");
System.out.println(p.getFileSystem().equals(FileSystems.getDefault()));
} }

cards.front: Which method creates a symbolic link?
cards.extra: The target need not exist, which is what makes dangling symbolic links possible.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
Path link = Files.createSymbolicLink(Path.of("link.txt"), Path.of("target.txt"));
System.out.println(Files.isSymbolicLink(link));
} }

cards.front: Which method creates a hard link?
cards.extra: The target must exist, otherwise NoSuchFileException. Hard links are also generally forbidden on directories and across volumes.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
Path link = Files.createLink(Path.of("hard.txt"), Path.of("a.txt"));
System.out.println(Files.isSameFile(link, Path.of("a.txt")));
} }

cards.front: What happens when you call readSymbolicLink() on a path that is not a link?
cards.extra: Use isSymbolicLink(Path) first if the path type is unknown. readSymbolicLink returns the link's target, not its content.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
Path p = Files.createTempFile("t", ".txt");
try { Files.readSymbolicLink(p); } catch (NotLinkException e) { System.out.println("not a link"); }
} }

cards.front: How does a hard link differ from a symbolic link in what it is?
cards.back: A hard link is the same entity as the original file, with identical attributes
cards.extra: Both names refer to one inode, so a write through either is visible through the other and the data survives until the last name is deleted.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
Path original = Path.of("a.txt"), hard = Files.createLink(Path.of("hard.txt"), original);
System.out.println(Files.isSameFile(original, hard) + " " + Files.readAttributes(hard, java.nio.file.attribute.BasicFileAttributes.class).fileKey());
} }

cards.front: Can a hard link point to a file that does not exist?
cards.extra: That is the opposite of a symbolic link, whose target is only resolved when it is followed.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
Path target = Files.createFile(Path.of("target.txt")); // target must already exist
Files.createLink(Path.of("hard.txt"), target);
} }

cards.front: Which method lists a directory's entries as a DirectoryStream?
cards.extra: The stream is Iterable, so it works in an enhanced for loop, and it scales to very large directories because entries are read lazily.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*; import java.io.IOException;
class Ex { static void m() throws IOException {
try (DirectoryStream ds = Files.newDirectoryStream(Path.of("."))) {
for (Path p : ds) System.out.println(p);
} } }

cards.front: What must you do with a DirectoryStream after use?
cards.extra: A try-with-resources statement is the standard way. Forgetting to close leaks handles, especially when iteration stops early.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
try (DirectoryStream ds = Files.newDirectoryStream(Path.of("."))) {
for (Path p : ds) System.out.println(p);
} } }

cards.front: How are entries returned by newDirectoryStream() shaped?
cards.back: As paths resolved against the listed directory, such as /tmp/a
cards.extra: They are not bare names, so you can use them directly for metadata calls without re-joining the directory.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
try (DirectoryStream ds = Files.newDirectoryStream(Path.of("/tmp/a"))) {
for (Path entry : ds) System.out.println(entry); // /tmp/a/child, not just "child"
} } }

cards.front: What exception do you need to handle during a DirectoryStream iteration?
cards.back: DirectoryIteratorException, wrapping the IOException as its cause
cards.extra: Iterator methods cannot declare checked exceptions, so the I/O failure is wrapped and thrown unchecked.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*; import java.io.IOException;
class Ex { static void m() {
try { throw new DirectoryIteratorException(new IOException("read failed")); }
catch (DirectoryIteratorException e) { System.out.println(e.getCause().getClass().getSimpleName()); }
} }

cards.front: Which method lists only entries whose names match a glob pattern?
cards.extra: The two-argument overload compiles the pattern for you. Use the Filter overload for conditions that are not name-based.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
try (DirectoryStream ds = Files.newDirectoryStream(Path.of("."), "*.java")) {
for (Path p : ds) System.out.println(p);
} } }

cards.front: In glob syntax, what does a single * match that ** does not?
cards.back: * matches any characters within one name; ** also crosses directory boundaries
cards.extra: That is why ** is used for complete path patterns such as **/*.java, while *.java stays in one directory.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
var one = FileSystems.getDefault().getPathMatcher("glob:*.java");
var all = FileSystems.getDefault().getPathMatcher("glob:**/*.java");
System.out.println(one.matches(Path.of("a/B.java")) + " " + all.matches(Path.of("a/B.java")));
} }

cards.front: In glob syntax, what does ? match?
cards.extra: So ??? matches every name of exactly three characters, and a?*.java requires at least one character after the a.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
PathMatcher m = FileSystems.getDefault().getPathMatcher("glob:?.txt");
System.out.println(m.matches(Path.of("a.txt")) + " " + m.matches(Path.of("ab.txt")));
} }

cards.front: In glob syntax, what does the brace form {htm,html,pdf} mean?
cards.back: Match any one of the listed subpatterns
cards.extra: So *.{htm,html,pdf} takes files with any of the three extensions, which saves writing three separate patterns.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
var g = FileSystems.getDefault().getPathMatcher("glob:*.{htm,html,pdf}");
System.out.println(g.matches(Path.of("a.html")) + " " + g.matches(Path.of("a.txt")));
} }

cards.front: How do you filter a directory listing by something other than the name?
cards.back: Implement DirectoryStream.Filter and pass it to newDirectoryStream
cards.extra: Its single accept() method decides per entry, typically by calling a metadata check such as isDirectory().
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*; import java.io.IOException;
class Ex { static void m() throws IOException {
DirectoryStream.Filter dirs = p -> java.nio.file.Files.isDirectory(p);
try (DirectoryStream s = Files.newDirectoryStream(Path.of("."), dirs)) { s.forEach(System.out::println); }
} }

cards.front: Why prefer Files.readAttributes() over repeated single-attribute calls?
cards.back: It fetches all attributes in one bulk operation, not one system call each
cards.extra: Each single-attribute call can hit the disk or the network, so a loop over files can cost orders of magnitude more.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.nio.file.attribute.BasicFileAttributes;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
BasicFileAttributes a = Files.readAttributes(Path.of("a.txt"), BasicFileAttributes.class);
System.out.println(a.size() + " " + a.lastModifiedTime() + " " + a.isRegularFile());
} }

cards.front: What is a file attribute view?
cards.back: A grouping of related attributes mapped to a file system flavor such as POSIX or DOS
cards.extra: File systems differ in which attributes they track, so views let one API serve all of them. Basic is the common denominator.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.nio.file.attribute.PosixFileAttributes;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
PosixFileAttributes a = Files.readAttributes(Path.of("x"), PosixFileAttributes.class);
System.out.println(a.owner());
} }

cards.front: Which attribute view supplies file owner, group owner and nine permission bits?
cards.extra: It extends the basic view for POSIX standards. DOS systems instead use the four attribute bits of DosFileAttributeView.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.nio.file.attribute.PosixFileAttributeView;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
PosixFileAttributeView view = Files.getFileAttributeView(Path.of("x"), PosixFileAttributeView.class);
System.out.println(view);
} }

cards.front: What does the nine-digit POSIX permission string rw-r--r-- describe?
cards.back: Read/write for owner, read-only for group, read-only for everyone else
cards.extra: PosixFilePermissions.toString() produces exactly this form, and fromString() parses it back into a Set.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*; import java.nio.file.attribute.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
var perms = PosixFilePermissions.fromString("rw-r--r--");
System.out.println(PosixFilePermissions.toString(perms)); // rw-r--r--
} }

cards.front: Which class method turns a permission set into a FileAttribute for file creation?
cards.extra: Pass the result to Files.createFile or createDirectory. The umask still applies, so the final file can be more restrictive.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.nio.file.attribute.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
java.util.Set<PosixFilePermission> perms = PosixFilePermissions.fromString("rw-r--r--");
Files.createFile(Path.of("a.txt"), PosixFilePermissions.asFileAttribute(perms));
} }

cards.front: Which method determines a file's MIME type?
cards.extra: It depends on the platform detector and can be fooled, for example by a .class extension. It returns null when the type is unknown.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
System.out.println(Files.probeContentType(Path.of("a.txt")));
} }

cards.front: What does BasicFileAttributes.fileKey() return?
cards.back: An object uniquely identifying the file, or null if unavailable
cards.extra: Use it to compare two paths for identity when you do not want to resolve symbolic links just to run isSameFile().
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*; import java.nio.file.attribute.BasicFileAttributes;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
BasicFileAttributes a = Files.readAttributes(Path.of("a.txt"), BasicFileAttributes.class);
System.out.println(a.fileKey()); // unique id, or null if unavailable
} }

cards.front: Which three timestamps does the basic attribute view expose?
cards.extra: Any of them may be unsupported by an implementation, in which case the accessor returns an implementation-specific value.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.nio.file.attribute.BasicFileAttributes;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
BasicFileAttributes a = Files.readAttributes(Path.of("a.txt"), BasicFileAttributes.class);
System.out.println(a.creationTime() + " " + a.lastModifiedTime() + " " + a.lastAccessTime());
} }

cards.front: Which helper class looks up a name as a UserPrincipal for setting a file owner?
cards.extra: It converts a user name or group name string into the principal object that Files.setOwner() expects.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.nio.file.attribute.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
UserPrincipalLookupService lookup = FileSystems.getDefault().getUserPrincipalLookupService();
Files.setOwner(Path.of("a.txt"), lookup.lookupPrincipalByName("alice")); // name -> principal
} }

cards.front: What does Files.exists() and Files.notExists() both returning false mean?
cards.back: The file's status is unknown, for example because the program cannot access it
cards.extra: Existence has three outcomes. That is why !Files.exists(p) is not equivalent to Files.notExists(p).
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
Path p = Path.of("maybe");
boolean unknown = !Files.exists(p) && !Files.notExists(p); // both false => unknown
System.out.println(unknown);
} }

cards.front: Which two-argument method tells whether two paths locate the same file?
cards.extra: It resolves symbolic links, so two different paths to one target return true. It declares IOException, unlike equals().
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
Path a = Path.of("a.txt"), b = Path.of("./a.txt");
System.out.println(Files.isSameFile(a, b));
} }

cards.front: What does Files.delete() do when the target does not exist?
cards.extra: Use deleteIfExists() when concurrent threads may be deleting the same file, so a missing file is not an error.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
try { Files.delete(Path.of("missing.txt")); }
catch (NoSuchFileException e) { System.out.println("no such file"); }
} }

cards.front: What does Files.copy() do with the contents of a source directory?
cards.back: It copies the directory only - the new directory is empty
cards.extra: A recursive copy needs walkFileTree(). The same applies to move(): emptying a directory elsewhere is not part of the operation.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
Path src = Files.createTempDirectory("src"), dst = Files.createTempDirectory("out").resolve("copy");
Files.copy(src, dst);
try (var s = Files.list(dst)) { System.out.println(s.count() + " entries in the copy"); }
} }

cards.front: Which copy option copies the source's metadata, including last-modified time, to the target?
cards.extra: Exact support is platform dependent, but last-modified time works across platforms and is the usual reason to need it.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
Files.copy(Path.of("a.txt"), Path.of("b.txt"), StandardCopyOption.COPY_ATTRIBUTES);
System.out.println(Files.getLastModifiedTime(Path.of("b.txt")));
} }

cards.front: What does NOFOLLOW_LINKS do when copying a symbolic link?
cards.back: Copies the link itself, not the file it points to
cards.extra: Without it the link is followed and the target's content is copied, which can silently duplicate a large file.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
Path link = Path.of("link"), copy = Path.of("copy"); Files.createSymbolicLink(link, Path.of("target.txt"));
Files.copy(link, copy, LinkOption.NOFOLLOW_LINKS);
System.out.println(Files.isSymbolicLink(copy));
} }

cards.front: What does ATOMIC_MOVE guarantee about a move?
cards.back: It cannot be interrupted or partially performed - either it happens or it fails
cards.extra: The file-system must support it or an exception is thrown. This is what lets a watcher see only complete files arrive.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
import static java.nio.file.StandardCopyOption.ATOMIC_MOVE;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
Files.move(Path.of("a.txt"), Path.of("b.txt"), ATOMIC_MOVE); // all-or-nothing move
} }

cards.front: On UNIX, can move() relocate a non-empty directory?
cards.back: Yes, when it is a rename inside the same partition
cards.extra: The contents are never relocated: the directory entry is simply renamed, so nothing has to be copied or emptied.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
Path d = Files.createTempDirectory("d");
Files.createFile(d.resolve("child.txt")); // non-empty directory
Files.move(d, d.resolveSibling("renamed")); // UNIX: rename within one partition
} }

cards.front: What is a varargs parameter in a method signature such as copy(Path, Path, CopyOption...)?
cards.back: A method parameter that accepts a comma-separated list or an array of values
cards.extra: Both call styles compile identically, so copy(a, b, opts) with a CopyOption[] variable is valid.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
Files.copy(Path.of("a.txt"), Path.of("b.txt"), StandardCopyOption.REPLACE_EXISTING, StandardCopyOption.COPY_ATTRIBUTES);
Files.copy(Path.of("a.txt"), Path.of("c.txt"), new CopyOption[] {StandardCopyOption.REPLACE_EXISTING});
} }
