cards.front: Which method removes redundant . and dir/.. elements from a path?
cards.extra: It is purely syntactic and never checks the file system, so on a path containing a symlink it can point at the wrong file.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
Path p = Path.of("./a/b/../c");
System.out.println(p.normalize());
} }

cards.front: Why can normalize() produce a wrong path when a symlink is involved?
cards.back: It never consults the file system, so link/.. may not be the parent
cards.extra: toRealPath() is the fix: it resolves symlinks and returns the true location of an existing file.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
Path link = Path.of("link/..");
System.out.println(link.normalize()); // textual only, does not consult the file system
System.out.println(link.toRealPath()); // resolves symlinks
} }

cards.front: Which method returns the real path of an existing file with symlinks resolved?
cards.extra: It also makes a relative path absolute and drops redundant elements. It throws if the file does not exist or cannot be accessed.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
Path real = Path.of("a.txt").toRealPath(); // symlinks resolved, absolute, existing
} }

cards.front: Does toAbsolutePath() require the file to exist?
cards.back: No - it only resolves against the working directory
cards.extra: That makes it safe for user-entered names before the file is created. Only toRealPath() needs the file to exist.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
Path p = Path.of("no-such-file.txt").toAbsolutePath();
System.out.println(p + " exists=" + Files.exists(p));
} }

cards.front: What does path.resolve(other) do with an absolute other path?
cards.back: Returns the argument unchanged, discarding the receiver
cards.extra: Appending an absolute path makes the base irrelevant, which is the usual reason resolve() appears to lose part of a path.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
Path base = Path.of("/tmp/a");
Path out = base.resolve(Path.of("/other/b"));
System.out.println(out); // /other/b: base discarded
} }

cards.front: Which method builds a relative path from one location to another?
cards.extra: It needs both paths with or without a root: if only one has one, no relative path can be formed, and IllegalArgumentException follows.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
Path a = Path.of("/a/b"), b = Path.of("/a/b/c/d");
System.out.println(a.relativize(b));
} }

cards.front: Can relativize() work when only one of the two paths has a root element?
cards.back: Refuses - you need both or neither path to have a root
cards.extra: For two relative paths the result expresses how to walk from one to the other, such as ../sally/bar.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
Path abs = Path.of("/a/b"), rel = Path.of("c/d");
try { abs.relativize(rel); } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { System.out.println(e.getClass().getSimpleName()); }
} }

cards.front: When do two Path objects compare equal with equals()?
cards.back: When their name elements match - the comparison is file system dependent
cards.extra: Two different paths can still locate one file through a symlink, so use Files.isSameFile() to test location rather than text.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
boolean equal = Path.of("/tmp/a").equals(Path.of("/tmp/a")); // matching name elements
boolean same = Files.isSameFile(Path.of("/tmp/a"), Path.of("/tmp/link")); // same location
} }

cards.front: Which method gives the number of name elements in a Path, excluding the root?
cards.extra: Index 0 is farthest from the root, so getName(0) is the highest directory in the path.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
Path p = Path.of("/tmp/a/b.txt");
System.out.println(p.getNameCount()); // 3 name elements, root excluded
} }

cards.front: What does getRoot() return for a relative path?
cards.extra: An absolute path returns its root, such as / on UNIX or C:\ on Windows. A relative path has no root element at all.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
System.out.println(Path.of("a/b.txt").getRoot()); // null
System.out.println(Path.of("/a/b.txt").getRoot()); // /
} }

cards.front: Which two interfaces does Path extend beyond the usual, enabling for-each and sorting?
cards.extra: Iteration visits name elements from the one nearest the root outwards, and compareTo() supports ordering paths in collections.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
java.lang.Iterable it = Path.of("a", "b");
java.lang.Comparable cmp = Path.of("a");
java.util.List ps = new java.util.ArrayList<>(); for (Path p : it) ps.add(p); java.util.Collections.sort(ps);
} }

cards.front: Which four callbacks make up the FileVisitor interface?
cards.extra: They fire before a directory, after it, on each file, and when an entry cannot be accessed.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
java.nio.file.FileVisitor v = new java.nio.file.SimpleFileVisitor() {
public java.nio.file.FileVisitResult preVisitDirectory(Path d, java.nio.file.attribute.BasicFileAttributes a) { return java.nio.file.FileVisitResult.CONTINUE; } public java.nio.file.FileVisitResult postVisitDirectory(Path d, java.io.IOException e) { return java.nio.file.FileVisitResult.CONTINUE; }
public java.nio.file.FileVisitResult visitFile(Path f, java.nio.file.attribute.BasicFileAttributes a) { return java.nio.file.FileVisitResult.CONTINUE; } public java.nio.file.FileVisitResult visitFileFailed(Path f, java.io.IOException e) { return java.nio.file.FileVisitResult.CONTINUE; } };
} }

cards.front: Which class should you extend when you need only one or two of the four FileVisitor methods?
cards.extra: It implements FileVisitor with sane defaults - CONTINUE for the others - and rethrows errors as IOError.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
Files.walkFileTree(Path.of("dir"), new java.nio.file.SimpleFileVisitor() {
public java.nio.file.FileVisitResult visitFile(Path f, java.nio.file.attribute.BasicFileAttributes a) { System.out.println(f); return java.nio.file.FileVisitResult.CONTINUE; }
}); } }

cards.front: Which callback should a recursive delete use to remove each directory?
cards.extra: Files must be gone before the directory that contains them, and post-visit runs after all entries have been handled.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
Files.walkFileTree(Path.of("dir"), new java.nio.file.SimpleFileVisitor() {
public java.nio.file.FileVisitResult visitFile(Path f, java.nio.file.attribute.BasicFileAttributes a) throws java.io.IOException { Files.delete(f); return java.nio.file.FileVisitResult.CONTINUE; }
public java.nio.file.FileVisitResult postVisitDirectory(Path d, java.io.IOException e) throws java.io.IOException { Files.delete(d); return java.nio.file.FileVisitResult.CONTINUE; }
}); } }

cards.front: Which callback should a recursive copy use to create the target directory?
cards.extra: The directory has to exist before files can be written into it. Attributes are best applied in postVisitDirectory, after copying.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.nio.file.attribute.BasicFileAttributes;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
Path src = Path.of("src"), dst = Path.of("dst");
Files.walkFileTree(src, new SimpleFileVisitor() {
public FileVisitResult preVisitDirectory(Path d, BasicFileAttributes a) throws IOException {
Files.createDirectories(dst.resolve(src.relativize(d))); return FileVisitResult.CONTINUE; }
}); } }

cards.front: Where must a file search do its comparison to also match directories?
cards.extra: visitFile only sees files. Directories are visited exclusively by the pre and post callbacks, so a policy applied only there misses them.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
var v = new SimpleFileVisitor<Path>() {
public FileVisitResult visitFile(Path p, java.nio.file.attribute.BasicFileAttributes a) { if (p.toString().equals("x")) System.out.println(p); return FileVisitResult.CONTINUE; }
public FileVisitResult preVisitDirectory(Path d, java.nio.file.attribute.BasicFileAttributes a) { if (d.toString().equals("x")) System.out.println(d); return FileVisitResult.CONTINUE; } };
Files.walkFileTree(Path.of("."), v); } }

cards.front: By default, does walkFileTree() follow symbolic links?
cards.back: No - you must pass the FOLLOW_LINKS visit option
cards.extra: Following links while deleting is especially risky, since the delete can escape the tree entirely.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.util.EnumSet;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
Files.walkFileTree(Path.of("dir"), EnumSet.of(FileVisitOption.FOLLOW_LINKS), Integer.MAX_VALUE, new SimpleFileVisitor() { });
} }

cards.front: Which FileVisitResult prunes a directory and everything under it?
cards.extra: Returned from preVisitDirectory, it removes that branch from the traversal, the equivalent of find's -prune.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
Files.walkFileTree(Path.of("."), new SimpleFileVisitor<Path>() {
public FileVisitResult preVisitDirectory(Path d, java.nio.file.attribute.BasicFileAttributes a) { return FileVisitResult.SKIP_SUBTREE; }
}); } }

cards.front: What does returning SKIP_SIBLINGS from visitFile do?
cards.back: Skips the remaining siblings - no other file or directory beside it is visited
cards.extra: Returned from preVisitDirectory it also skips that directory and no postVisitDirectory is called for it.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.nio.file.attribute.BasicFileAttributes;
class Ex extends SimpleFileVisitor {
public FileVisitResult visitFile(Path f, BasicFileAttributes a) {
return FileVisitResult.SKIP_SIBLINGS; // skip remaining siblings
} }

cards.front: Which callback reports a circular symbolic link when following links?
cards.extra: This is the only way a follow-links walk can terminate on a loop, so handle it there or the walk fails.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
Files.walkFileTree(Path.of("dir"), new java.nio.file.SimpleFileVisitor() {
public java.nio.file.FileVisitResult visitFileFailed(Path p, java.io.IOException e) { if (e instanceof FileSystemLoopException) System.out.println("circular link: " + p); return java.nio.file.FileVisitResult.CONTINUE; }
}); } }

cards.front: What must you pass as depth to walkFileTree to visit the whole tree?
cards.extra: The four-argument overload caps the traversal at that many levels, so an explicit maximum is the 'unlimited' spelling.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
Files.walkFileTree(Path.of("dir"), java.util.Set.of(), Integer.MAX_VALUE, new java.nio.file.SimpleFileVisitor() {});
System.out.println("whole tree visited");
} }

cards.front: What is the single method defined by PathMatcher?
cards.extra: Fetch one from FileSystem.getPathMatcher("glob:...") or "regex:...". Glob is the usual choice for file names.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
PathMatcher matcher = FileSystems.getDefault().getPathMatcher("glob:*.txt");
boolean hit = matcher.matches(Path.of("a.txt")); // its single method
} }

cards.front: Which method creates a WatchService for a file system?
cards.extra: It is obtained from a FileSystem such as FileSystems.getDefault(), not from the Files class.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
WatchService ws = FileSystems.getDefault().newWatchService();
System.out.println(ws.getClass().getSimpleName());
ws.close();
} }

cards.front: Which three entry event kinds can you register with a watch service?
cards.extra: A fourth, OVERFLOW, arrives whether or not you register for it, because it signals lost events.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
var ws = FileSystems.getDefault().newWatchService();
var key = Path.of(".").register(ws, StandardWatchEventKinds.ENTRY_CREATE, StandardWatchEventKinds.ENTRY_DELETE, StandardWatchEventKinds.ENTRY_MODIFY);
System.out.println(key.pollEvents());
} }

cards.front: Which method blocks until a watch key is available?
cards.extra: poll() returns null immediately when nothing is queued; poll(long, TimeUnit) waits at most that long.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
WatchService ws = FileSystems.getDefault().newWatchService();
WatchKey key = ws.take(); // blocks until a key is available
} }

cards.front: Why is WatchKey.reset() mandatory at the end of each event cycle?
cards.back: Without it the key stays signaled and receives no further events
cards.extra: After processing, put the key back into the ready state. A false return means the key was invalidated, so the loop can end.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
WatchService ws = FileSystems.getDefault().newWatchService();
WatchKey key = Path.of(".").register(ws, StandardWatchEventKinds.ENTRY_MODIFY);
for (WatchEvent e : key.pollEvents()) System.out.println(e.kind()); key.reset(); // without reset the key stays signaled and receives no further events
} }

cards.front: What should you check for in every event, even if you did not register for it?
cards.extra: It means events may have been dropped, so a count-sensitive listener must reconcile the directory rather than trust the stream.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
import static java.nio.file.StandardWatchEventKinds.*;
class Ex { static void m(WatchEvent event) {
if (event.kind() == OVERFLOW) { /* events were lost */ }
} }

cards.front: When does a watch key enter the invalid state?
cards.back: On cancel(), when the directory becomes inaccessible, or when the service closes
cards.extra: An invalid key delivers nothing further. Reset() returning false is how your loop detects it.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*; import java.io.IOException;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
WatchService ws = FileSystems.getDefault().newWatchService();
WatchKey key = Path.of(".").register(ws, StandardWatchEventKinds.ENTRY_CREATE);
key.cancel(); System.out.println(key.isValid()); // false: cancel invalidates
} }

cards.front: How do you recover the changed file's name from a WatchEvent?
cards.back: event.context() yields the entry, which is a Path
cards.extra: The context type is untyped, so the cast to WatchEvent<Path> needs suppression of the unchecked warning.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
WatchService ws = FileSystems.getDefault().newWatchService();
Path dir = Path.of("."); dir.register(ws, StandardWatchEventKinds.ENTRY_CREATE);
WatchKey key = ws.poll(); for (WatchEvent e : key.pollEvents()) System.out.println((Path) e.context());
} }

cards.front: What are watch keys noted as being, enabling a dedicated thread pool to process them?
cards.back: Thread-safe - they work with the java.util.concurrent package
cards.extra: You may keep one watcher thread, as the bundled example does, or distribute keys across a pool for heavy event rates.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
WatchService ws = FileSystems.getDefault().newWatchService();
java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService pool = java.util.concurrent.Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor();
pool.submit(() -> { WatchKey k = ws.poll(); if (k != null) { for (WatchEvent e : k.pollEvents()) System.out.println(e.context()); k.reset(); } });
} }

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.front: Which four abstract base classes define the Java I/O stream model?
cards.extra: Reader/Writer handle characters, InputStream/OutputStream handle bytes. Everything else in java.io descends from these four.
cards.example:
import java.io.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
Reader r = new StringReader("x"); Writer w = new StringWriter();
InputStream in = new ByteArrayInputStream(new byte[1]); OutputStream out = new ByteArrayOutputStream();
System.out.println(r.getClass() + " " + w.getClass() + " " + in.getClass() + " " + out.getClass());
} }

cards.front: What does NIO stand for today, and what did it originally stand for?
cards.extra: It arrived in Java SE 1.4 with channels and buffers. The renaming reflects what the feature actually delivered.
cards.example:
class Ex { static void m() {
String now = "Non-blocking I/O";
String originally = "New I/O"; // what NIO meant when introduced in Java SE 1.4
} }

cards.front: Why did the Path interface replace the File class?
cards.back: Methods returned false on failure, with no symlink support and poor scaling
cards.extra: Path fixes error reporting through exceptions, adds metadata and link support, and streams huge directory listings safely.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*; import java.io.File;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
boolean ok = new File("a").delete(); // false gives no reason; Files.delete throws it
System.out.println(Files.isSymbolicLink(Path.of("a"))); // links are explicit
try (var paths = Files.walk(Path.of("."))) { System.out.println(paths.count()); }
} }

cards.front: Which pattern describes the shape of every I/O stream?
cards.back: A sequence of data, read or written one item at a time
cards.extra: Sources can be files, devices, sockets or arrays; the model is uniform regardless of what the stream internally transforms.
cards.example:
import java.io.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
InputStream in = new ByteArrayInputStream(new byte[] { 1, 2, 3 });
int item; while ((item = in.read()) != -1) System.out.println(item);
} }

cards.front: What are the two kinds of content the Java I/O API distinguishes?
cards.back: Character content (text, XML, JSON) and byte content (images, video)
cards.extra: Each content kind crossed with reading or writing gives the four base classes of the stream hierarchy.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
Files.writeString(Path.of("text.txt"), "XML, JSON");
Files.write(Path.of("image.bin"), new byte[] {1, 2, 3});
} }

cards.front: What is the difference between an I/O stream and a java.util.stream?
cards.back: Unrelated concepts that only share a name, used for completely different jobs
cards.extra: The collision causes real confusion, so it is worth stating explicitly that neither is a specialization of the other.
cards.example:
import java.io.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
InputStream io = new ByteArrayInputStream(new byte[] { 1 });
java.util.stream.Stream util = java.util.stream.Stream.of("a");
System.out.println(io.getClass().getSimpleName() + " vs " + util.getClass().getSimpleName());
} }

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.front: Why does SonnetReader extend BufferedReader?
cards.back: It reuses line reading and gets automatic closing from try-with-resources
cards.extra: The subclass adds skipLines(), skipSonnetHeader() and readNextSonnet(), while close() is inherited from BufferedReader.
cards.example:
import java.io.*;
class Ex {
static class SonnetReader extends BufferedReader {
SonnetReader(Reader r) { super(r); }
String readNextSonnet() throws IOException { return readLine(); }
}
static void m() throws Exception { try (var r = new SonnetReader(new StringReader("first\n"))) { System.out.println(r.readNextSonnet()); } }
}

cards.front: When extending a resource-holding class, what must an overriding close() do?
cards.back: Call the superclass close() so the wrapped resources are released
cards.extra: If you skip it, the delegate such as a BufferedReader over a FileReader leaks its file handle.
cards.example:
import java.io.*;
class Ex { static class Wrapper extends FilterOutputStream {
Wrapper(OutputStream out) { super(out); }
public void close() throws IOException { super.close(); }
} }

cards.front: When reading a compressed sonnet, which classes are composed in order from bytes to lines?
cards.extra: Binary decorations strip the compression, the character stream decodes the bytes, and the buffer supplies line reads.
cards.example:
import java.io.*; import java.util.zip.GZIPInputStream;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
try (var gz = new GZIPInputStream(new ByteArrayInputStream(new byte[0]));
var lines = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(gz))) {
System.out.println(lines.readLine());
} } }

cards.front: When writing a compressed sonnet, which classes wrap a ByteArrayOutputStream?
cards.extra: Closest to the bytes is the compressor, closest to your code is the writer. Println is convenient because PrintWriter supplies it.
cards.example:
import java.io.*;
import java.util.zip.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
try (var w = new PrintWriter(new OutputStreamWriter(new GZIPOutputStream(new ByteArrayOutputStream()), "UTF-8"))) {
w.println("sonnet"); } // PrintWriter -> GZIPOutputStream -> bytes
} }

cards.front: How many sonnets does the Shakespeare example file contain?
cards.extra: The first four bytes of the file hold that count, then per sonnet an offset and a length, then the compressed texts.
cards.example:
class Ex { static void m() {
int sonnets = 154; // the count stored in the Shakespeare file
System.out.println(sonnets);
} }

cards.front: Why can a single skip(n) call on an I/O stream fall short?
cards.back: It may skip fewer bytes than asked, so loop until the count is reached
cards.extra: The stream cannot be trusted to buffer arbitrary lengths, so a fixed skip is a loop that accumulates what was actually skipped.
cards.example:
import java.io.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
try (InputStream in = new FileInputStream("a.bin")) {
long left = 10, skipped = 0;
while (left > 0) { long n = in.skip(left); if (n == 0) break; skipped += n; left -= n; }
System.out.println(skipped); } } }

cards.front: Which two streams write the sonnet file's header and payload?
cards.extra: Mixing them means decoration for the numbers and plain buffered writes for the compressed payload, in file-format order.
cards.example:
import java.io.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
ByteArrayOutputStream file = new ByteArrayOutputStream();
try (DataOutputStream head = new DataOutputStream(file)) { head.writeInt(1); }
try (BufferedOutputStream bytes = new BufferedOutputStream(file)) { bytes.write(new byte[] { 1, 2 }); }
} }

cards.front: In the sonnet file, what does each sonnet's length record?
cards.back: The number of bytes of that sonnet's compressed form
cards.extra: Sonnets vary in size, so each length must be stored. The offset points at the first byte of that compressed block.
cards.example:
class Ex { static void m() {
int[] lengths = new int[154]; // one length per sonnet
int i = 0;
int compressedBytes = lengths[i]; // bytes in that sonnet's compressed form
} }

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.front: Which method opens a file for reading bytes and returns an unbuffered InputStream?
cards.extra: Unbuffered means each read may hit the device, so wrapping in a BufferedInputStream is worth it for many small reads.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*; import java.io.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
try (InputStream in = Files.newInputStream(Path.of("a.txt"))) {
System.out.println(in.getClass().getName() + " " + in.read());
} } }

cards.front: Which method returns an unbuffered OutputStream for writing bytes?
cards.extra: With no options it creates the file if absent and truncates it if present, which equals CREATE plus TRUNCATE_EXISTING.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
try (java.io.OutputStream out = Files.newOutputStream(Path.of("a.txt"))) {
out.write(65);
} } }

cards.front: What is a SeekableByteChannel?
cards.back: A byte channel that keeps and can change a position in the file
cards.extra: It also supports truncate() and size(). Being seekable is what enables random access to a file.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.nio.channels.SeekableByteChannel;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
try (SeekableByteChannel ch = Files.newByteChannel(Path.of("a.txt"), StandardOpenOption.READ, StandardOpenOption.WRITE)) {
System.out.println(ch.position() + " " + ch.size()); ch.position(2L);
} } }

cards.front: How does channel I/O differ from stream I/O?
cards.back: Channel I/O moves a buffer at a time, stream I/O a byte or character at a time
cards.extra: Fewer per-item calls means channel I/O bypasses layers that bottleneck stream I/O.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.nio.channels.FileChannel;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
try (FileChannel ch = FileChannel.open(Path.of("a.txt"))) {
var buf = java.nio.ByteBuffer.allocate(64); int n = ch.read(buf); System.out.println(n);
} } }

cards.front: Which open option is required by newByteChannel() but not by newOutputStream()?
cards.extra: A seekable channel does both directions, so READ must be explicit. With no option at all the channel opens for reading.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.nio.channels.SeekableByteChannel;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
try (SeekableByteChannel ch = Files.newByteChannel(Path.of("a.txt"), StandardOpenOption.READ)) { System.out.println(ch.size()); }
try (var out = Files.newOutputStream(Path.of("b.txt"))) { out.write(1); }
} }

cards.front: What does FileChannel.open() add over newByteChannel()?
cards.back: Casting to FileChannel adds memory mapping, locking and absolute reads
cards.extra: On the default file system a newByteChannel() result can be cast to FileChannel to reach those advanced features.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.nio.channels.FileChannel;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
FileChannel ch = (FileChannel) Files.newByteChannel(Path.of("a.txt"), StandardOpenOption.READ);
var map = ch.map(FileChannel.MapMode.READ_ONLY, 0, ch.size());
System.out.println(map.get(0));
} }

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.front: Since which Java release is the default charset of an application UTF-8?
cards.extra: Before that the platform encoding was used, which could be a legacy Windows code page. Explicit charset parameters are now unnecessary.
cards.example:
import java.nio.charset.Charset;
class Ex { static void m() {
Charset cs = Charset.defaultCharset();
System.out.println(cs);
} }

cards.front: Which method opens a file for efficient line-oriented reading?
cards.extra: It returns a BufferedReader, whose readLine() gives lines without their terminator and null at end of file.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
try (var r = Files.newBufferedReader(Path.of("a.txt"), StandardCharsets.UTF_8)) {
System.out.println(r.readLine());
} } }

cards.front: How do you get a lazy Stream<String> of a file's lines since Java 8?
cards.extra: The stream is AutoCloseable, so open it in try-with-resources. Files.lines(Path) is the shortcut that skips the reader.
cards.example:
import java.io.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
try (BufferedReader r = new BufferedReader(new StringReader("a\nb"))) {
var lines = r.lines(); lines.forEach(System.out::println);
} } }

cards.front: Which method opens a file for buffered character writing?
cards.extra: The optional OpenOptions control creation and appending, so the same call can build a fresh file or extend an existing one.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
try (var w = Files.newBufferedWriter(Path.of("a.txt"), StandardCharsets.UTF_8)) {
w.write("text");
} } }

cards.front: What does BufferedReader.readLine() return at end of file?
cards.extra: Each returned line excludes its terminator, so a while loop testing for null is the classic line-reading pattern.
cards.example:
import java.io.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
BufferedReader r = new BufferedReader(new StringReader("one\n"));
System.out.println(r.readLine());
System.out.println(r.readLine()); // null at end of file
} }

cards.front: What did character streams do about the local charset before Java 18?
cards.back: Translated to and from the platform encoding automatically
cards.extra: That default could be a legacy Windows encoding, so code that needed to be portable passed StandardCharsets.UTF_8 explicitly.
cards.example:
import java.io.*;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
Reader implicit = new FileReader("a.txt"); // used the platform encoding before Java 18
Reader explicit = new InputStreamReader(new FileInputStream("a.txt"), StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
} }

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.front: What single checked exception type do all file I/O operations throw?
cards.extra: More specific subclasses exist, such as FileNotFoundException and DirectoryNotEmptyException, and may need handling too.
cards.example:
import java.io.IOException;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;
class Ex { static void m() throws IOException {
Files.readString(Path.of("a.txt"));
} }

cards.front: Which Java release introduced try-with-resources?
cards.extra: It calls close() on each declared resource as the block exits, normally or exceptionally, so no finally block is needed.
cards.example:
import java.io.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
try (Reader r = new StringReader("x")) { System.out.println(r.read()); } // since Java SE 7
} }

cards.front: In what order does try-with-resources close multiple resources?
cards.back: In reverse order of declaration - the last declared closes first
cards.extra: So a BufferedReader declared over an InputStream closes first, releasing the outer layer before the underlying stream.
cards.example:
import java.io.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
try (Closeable a = () -> System.out.println("first"); Closeable b = () -> System.out.println("last")) { }
} }

cards.front: Which methods does FileSystemException provide for diagnosis?
cards.extra: The last is for two-file operations such as copy, where both the source and the target matter to understand the failure.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.FileSystemException;
class Ex { static void m() {
FileSystemException e = new FileSystemException("a.txt", "b.txt", "denied");
System.out.println(e.getFile() + " " + e.getReason() + " " + e.getMessage() + " " + e.getOtherFile());
} }

cards.front: What is method chaining?
cards.back: Calling the next method on the object returned by the previous call
cards.extra: It avoids temporary variables and keeps I/O setup readable, for example chaining getPath() onto getDefault().
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
String s = Path.of("dir", "file.txt").getFileName().toString().toUpperCase();
System.out.println(s);
} }

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.front: Which design pattern does the Java I/O API use to extend stream behavior?
cards.extra: A wrapper object takes the delegate stream in its constructor and adds or overrides behavior without altering the wrapped class.
cards.example:
import java.io.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
Reader r = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("a.txt"));
System.out.println(r.getClass().getSimpleName());
} }

cards.front: Which class reads characters from an InputStream?
cards.extra: It is a Reader over bytes. FileReader is a convenience subclass that opens a file directly.
cards.example:
import java.io.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
Reader r = new InputStreamReader(new FileInputStream("a.bin")); // chars from bytes
} }

cards.front: Which class writes characters to an OutputStream?
cards.extra: It is a Writer for byte sinks. Its close() flushes the encoded characters before closing the stream.
cards.example:
import java.io.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
ByteArrayOutputStream bytes = new ByteArrayOutputStream();
try (Writer w = new OutputStreamWriter(bytes)) { w.write("hi"); }
System.out.println(bytes.toString());
} }

cards.front: What can happen if a writer wrapping an output stream is never flushed?
cards.back: Characters stay in the internal buffer and are missing from the file
cards.extra: try-with-resources closes both in the right order, flushing each layer as it goes, which is why omitting it is a real data-loss bug.
cards.example:
import java.io.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
PrintWriter w = new PrintWriter(new FileWriter("a.txt"));
w.print("text"); // still in the buffer: absent from the file until flush/close
} }

cards.front: Which two classes add primitive read and write methods to a binary stream?
cards.extra: They write and read int, long, double and so on in a fixed binary encoding, which is what a binary file format needs.
cards.example:
import java.io.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
try (DataOutputStream out = new DataOutputStream(new FileOutputStream("a.bin"))) { out.writeInt(42); }
try (DataInputStream in = new DataInputStream(new FileInputStream("a.bin"))) { System.out.println(in.readInt()); }
} }

cards.front: Why does writing six ints with DataOutputStream produce a 24-byte file?
cards.back: An int is 4 bytes, so six of them take 24
cards.extra: Unlike a text file, the binary encoding uses a fixed width per value, so the size is predictable from the count.
cards.example:
import java.io.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
ByteArrayOutputStream bytes = new ByteArrayOutputStream();
try (var out = new DataOutputStream(bytes)) { for (int i = 0; i < 6; i++) out.writeInt(i); }
System.out.println(bytes.size());
} }

cards.front: What does DataInputStream.readFully(byte[]) do at end of stream?
cards.back: Throws EOFException if the array cannot be filled
cards.extra: It blocks until the array is full, unlike plain read() which may return a partial count, so it is the right call for fixed-length records.
cards.example:
import java.io.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
DataInputStream in = new DataInputStream(new ByteArrayInputStream(new byte[] { 1 }));
try { in.readFully(new byte[2]); } catch (EOFException e) { System.out.println("short read"); }
} }

cards.front: What does DataOutputStream.writeUTF(String) use as its encoding?
cards.extra: readUTF() decodes the same format. Modified UTF-8 differs from standard UTF-8 in how it encodes the null character.
cards.example:
import java.io.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
ByteArrayOutputStream bytes = new ByteArrayOutputStream();
try (DataOutputStream out = new DataOutputStream(bytes)) { out.writeUTF("hi"); }
System.out.println(java.util.Arrays.toString(bytes.toByteArray())); // 0 2 h i
} }

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.front: Which class reads characters from a String?
cards.extra: CharArrayReader does the same over a char array. Both are Readers, so they plug into any buffered or parsing decoration.
cards.example:
import java.io.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws IOException {
try (StringReader r = new StringReader("abc")) { System.out.println((char) r.read()); }
} }

cards.front: How do you get the accumulated text from a StringWriter?
cards.extra: toString() builds a String from the internal StringBuffer, while getBuffer() exposes the buffer itself with no defensive copy.
cards.example:
import java.io.StringWriter;
class Ex { static void m() {
StringWriter w = new StringWriter(); w.write("hi");
System.out.println(w.toString() + " " + w.getBuffer().length());
} }

cards.front: Which class grows automatically and lets you read back the bytes written to it?
cards.extra: Set an initial size if known; size() gives the count, toByteArray() a copy, and toString() decodes using a charset.
cards.example:
import java.io.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
ByteArrayOutputStream out = new ByteArrayOutputStream();
out.write(new byte[] {1, 2, 3});
System.out.println(java.util.Arrays.toString(out.toByteArray()));
} }

cards.front: Why is a ByteArrayOutputStream useful when a file format needs a length field up front?
cards.back: You can serialize first and then ask size() for the byte count
cards.extra: Compressed content makes the length impossible to compute in advance, so writing to memory and measuring afterwards is the practical route.
cards.example:
import java.io.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
ByteArrayOutputStream buf = new ByteArrayOutputStream();
try (ObjectOutputStream out = new ObjectOutputStream(buf)) { out.writeObject("x"); }
System.out.println(buf.size());
} }

cards.front: Which class lets you build a String by appending characters through a Writer?
cards.extra: It wraps an internal StringBuffer, so repeated appends never copy the accumulated text the way string concatenation would.
cards.example:
import java.io.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
StringWriter sw = new StringWriter();
sw.write('h'); sw.write('i');
System.out.println(sw.toString());
} }

cards.front: Which three methods read back the content of a ByteArrayOutputStream?
cards.extra: size() gives the byte count, toByteArray() a defensive copy, and toString() decodes those bytes with the default or a given charset.
cards.example:
import java.io.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
ByteArrayOutputStream out = new ByteArrayOutputStream();
out.write('x');
System.out.println(out.size() + " " + java.util.Arrays.toString(out.toByteArray()) + " " + out.toString());
} }

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.front: Which method reads a whole small file into a byte[]?
cards.extra: It opens and closes the stream for you but is not meant for large files, since the entire content is held in memory.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
byte[] bytes = Files.readAllBytes(Path.of("a.txt"));
System.out.println(bytes.length);
} }

cards.front: Which method reads a whole small text file into a List<String>?
cards.extra: Lines come without terminators. For big files prefer Files.lines(), which processes the lines lazily.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
java.util.List<String> lines = Files.readAllLines(Path.of("a.txt"), StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
lines.forEach(System.out::println);
} }

cards.front: Which open option creates a new file and throws if it already exists?
cards.extra: CREATE instead opens an existing file or creates it. The difference decides whether an accidental overwrite is caught or allowed.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
Path p = Files.writeString(Path.of("new.txt"), "x", StandardOpenOption.CREATE_NEW);
try { Files.writeString(p, "y", StandardOpenOption.CREATE_NEW); }
catch (FileAlreadyExistsException e) { System.out.println("exists"); }
} }

cards.front: Which open option deletes the file when the stream closes?
cards.extra: It is designed for throwaway temporary files whose lifetime should never outlive the program's use of them.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
try (var out = Files.newOutputStream(Path.of("tmp.txt"), StandardOpenOption.CREATE, StandardOpenOption.DELETE_ON_CLOSE)) {
out.write(1);
} } }

cards.front: What does the SPARSE open option hint at?
cards.back: That the file will be sparse, so data gaps may consume no disk space
cards.extra: Only some file systems honor it, NTFS being the example given. It is a hint, so code must work when it is ignored.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
Files.newByteChannel(Path.of("sparse.bin"), StandardOpenOption.CREATE, StandardOpenOption.WRITE, StandardOpenOption.SPARSE);
System.out.println("SPARSE hints that data gaps may consume no disk space");
} }

cards.front: Why is Files.createFile() safer than an existence check followed by creation?
cards.back: The check and the creation happen in one atomic operation
cards.extra: A separate check leaves a window for another process to create the file first, a classic TOCTTOU race.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
Path p = Path.of("new.txt");
if (!Files.exists(p)) Files.createFile(p); // check-then-create is racy
Files.createFile(Path.of("atomic.txt")); // check and create in one atomic step
} }

cards.front: Which interface provides random access to a file through a movable position?
cards.extra: position() reads or sets the cursor, read/write move bytes through a ByteBuffer, and truncate() shortens the file.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*; import java.nio.channels.SeekableByteChannel; import java.nio.ByteBuffer;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
try (SeekableByteChannel ch = Files.newByteChannel(Path.of("a.txt"), StandardOpenOption.READ, StandardOpenOption.WRITE)) {
ch.position(4); ch.write(ByteBuffer.wrap(new byte[] { 1 })); ch.truncate(2);
} } }

cards.front: Which method creates an empty file in a single atomic step with preset attributes?
cards.extra: Files.write() also creates files but takes no attributes. Checking exists() and then creating is racy; createFile does both at once.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.nio.file.attribute.PosixFilePermissions;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
var attrs = PosixFilePermissions.asFileAttribute(PosixFilePermissions.fromString("rw-r-----"));
Files.createFile(Path.of("new.txt"), attrs); // created atomically with attributes
} }

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::01 I-O Operations

cards.front: Which single method reads a whole text file into a String?
cards.extra: Since Java 18 it assumes UTF-8, so no charset argument is needed. It opens and closes the file for you.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
String text = Files.readString(Path.of("a.txt"));
System.out.println(text);
} }

cards.front: Which method writes a String to a text file in one call?
cards.extra: For several lines use Files.writeString(path, list), and for binary data use Files.write with a byte array.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
Files.writeString(Path.of("a.txt"), "hello"); // writes a String in one call
} }

cards.front: Which method lazily streams a large file's lines, and what must you do with the result?
cards.extra: It holds the file handle open, so wrap it in try-with-resources. Files.readAllLines loads everything instead.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.util.stream.Stream;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
try (Stream lines = Files.lines(Path.of("a.txt"))) {
lines.forEach(System.out::println);
} } }

cards.front: Which method visits only the direct entries of a directory?
cards.extra: It returns a Stream<Path> that must be closed. Files.walk instead descends into subdirectories.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.util.stream.Stream;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
try (Stream<Path> s = Files.list(Path.of("."))) { s.forEach(System.out::println); }
} }

cards.front: Which method recursively visits a directory tree as a Stream?
cards.extra: An overload limits depth. Use stream operations such as filter and collect on the result, and close the stream.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.util.stream.Stream;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
try (Stream paths = Files.walk(Path.of("."))) { paths.forEach(System.out::println); }
} }

cards.front: Which method walks a tree giving each path free access to its BasicFileAttributes?
cards.extra: The predicate receives path and attributes together, which is cheaper than calling readAttributes separately per file.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.util.stream.Stream;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
try (Stream s = Files.find(Path.of("."), 2, (p, a) -> a.isRegularFile())) {
s.forEach(System.out::println);
} } }

cards.front: What does Files.walkFileTree offer that Files.walk does not?
cards.back: Notifications on first and last visit of a directory via a FileVisitor
cards.extra: That control matters when deleting or copying a whole tree, where the order of directory removal and creation is critical.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*; import java.nio.file.attribute.BasicFileAttributes;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
Files.walkFileTree(Path.of("."), new SimpleFileVisitor() {
public FileVisitResult preVisitDirectory(Path d, BasicFileAttributes a) { System.out.println("enter " + d); return FileVisitResult.CONTINUE; }
public FileVisitResult postVisitDirectory(Path d, java.io.IOException e) { System.out.println("leave " + d); return FileVisitResult.CONTINUE; }
}); } }

cards.front: Since which Java release can you mount a ZIP file as a file system?
cards.extra: Use FileSystems.newFileSystem to get one, then all Files methods work on its entries, and closing it writes the changes back.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
try (FileSystem zip = FileSystems.newFileSystem(Path.of("a.zip"))) {
System.out.println(zip.getPath("/"));
} } }

cards.front: What does closing a ZIP file system do?
cards.back: Writes the accumulated changes back into the ZIP file
cards.extra: All additions and deletions made through Files are held until then, so a crash before close loses them.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
FileSystem zip = FileSystems.newFileSystem(Path.of("a.zip"));
Files.writeString(zip.getPath("/x.txt"), "hi");
zip.close(); // accumulated changes are written back into a.zip
} }

cards.front: Which two classes provide the convenience methods for temporary files and directories?
cards.extra: They place the item in a suitable temporary location, such as /tmp on Linux, using the given prefix and optional suffix.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
Path f = Files.createTempFile("pre", ".txt");
Path d = Files.createTempDirectory("pre");
} }

cards.front: What is the modern replacement for reading a text file line by line with BufferedReader.readLine()?
cards.extra: getPathMatcher-era line loops obsolete. A stream of lines composes with filter and map directly.
cards.example:
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.util.stream.Stream;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
java.util.List<String> all = Files.readAllLines(Path.of("a.txt"));
try (Stream<String> lines = Files.lines(Path.of("a.txt"))) { lines.forEach(System.out::println); }
} }

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::04 Cryptography

cards.front: What is the difference between plaintext and ciphertext?
cards.back: Plaintext is readable; ciphertext is unreadable to an attacker
cards.extra: Encryption converts plaintext to ciphertext and decryption reverses it, using a publicly known algorithm plus a secret key.
cards.example:
try {
    javax.crypto.Cipher c = javax.crypto.Cipher.getInstance("AES");
    c.init(javax.crypto.Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, javax.crypto.KeyGenerator.getInstance("AES").generateKey());
    byte[] ciphertext = c.doFinal("readable plaintext".getBytes());   // unreadable to an attacker
} catch (Exception e) { }

cards.front: What does a cryptographic hash function produce from an arbitrarily long input?
cards.back: A fixed-length output, effectively unique to that input
cards.extra: Salting, concatenating random bits to the input, removes the ability to precompute a table that reverses common inputs.
cards.example:
try {
    byte[] a = java.security.MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256").digest(new byte[]{1});
    byte[] b = java.security.MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256").digest(new byte[10000]);   // same fixed length, effectively unique
} catch (Exception e) { }

cards.front: What is an initialization vector (IV) for?
cards.back: Adding cryptographic variance to the encryption of the first block of plaintext
cards.extra: Identical plaintext blocks encrypted with the same key would otherwise produce identical ciphertext, leaking structure.
cards.example:
byte[] ivBytes = new byte[16];   // adds cryptographic variance to the first plaintext block
javax.crypto.spec.IvParameterSpec iv = new javax.crypto.spec.IvParameterSpec(ivBytes);
System.out.println(iv.getIV().length);

cards.front: What does JCA stand for and what are its goals?
cards.back: Java Cryptography Architecture - algorithm independence and provider neutrality
cards.extra: It is the framework layer of the Java Security API; the actual algorithms live in pluggable providers.
cards.example:
String name = "Java Cryptography Architecture";   // JCA: algorithm independence, provider neutrality
System.out.println(name);

cards.front: Which pattern do you use to obtain a cryptographic implementation in the JCA?
cards.back: getInstance(algorithm) on an engine class, optionally plus a provider name
cards.extra: For example MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256") or with "ProviderC" pinned. The engine class is the service type.
cards.example:
try {
    java.security.MessageDigest md = java.security.MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256", "SUN");   // engine plus optional provider
    System.out.println(md.getAlgorithm());
} catch (Exception e) { }

cards.front: What are the three data states that encryption can protect?
cards.extra: At rest is stored data, in motion is data on the network, in use is data loaded and actively processed in memory.
cards.example:
import java.util.List;
class Ex { static void m() {
List<String> states = List.of("at rest", "in motion", "in use");
states.forEach(System.out::println);
} }

cards.front: In symmetric encryption, how many keys are involved?
cards.back: One shared key, used by both parties for encryption and decryption
cards.extra: Its cost is low, so it is the default for bulk data. The problem it does not solve is how to share the key safely.
cards.example:
try {
    javax.crypto.SecretKey key = javax.crypto.KeyGenerator.getInstance("AES").generateKey();
    System.out.println(key.getAlgorithm());   // one shared key encrypts and decrypts for both parties
} catch (Exception e) { }

cards.front: In asymmetric encryption, which key is used to encrypt a message to someone?
cards.extra: Only the matching private key can decrypt it. The private key also signs, which is verified with the public key.
cards.example:
try {
    java.security.KeyPair pair = java.security.KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("RSA").generateKeyPair();
    javax.crypto.Cipher c = javax.crypto.Cipher.getInstance("RSA");
    c.init(javax.crypto.Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, pair.getPublic());   // the recipient's public key
    byte[] msg = c.doFinal("hi".getBytes());
} catch (Exception e) { }

cards.front: Since which JDK release did the default AES key size rise from 128 to 256 bits?
cards.extra: Only when the installed crypto policy allows it; otherwise the default falls back to 128 bits.
cards.example:
int since = 19;   // default AES key size rose from 128 to 256 bits
System.out.println("JDK " + since);

cards.front: Which mode of operation combines a cipher with a counter and a Galois authenticator?
cards.extra: It provides confidentiality and integrity in one pass. ECB, by contrast, leaks repeated plaintext patterns.
cards.example:
String transformation = "AES/GCM/NoPadding";   // GCM = Galois/Counter Mode: counter plus Galois authenticator
System.out.println(transformation);

cards.front: What does Cipher.doFinal() do?
cards.back: Encrypts or decrypts in a single-part operation, or finishes a multiple-part one
cards.extra: It returns the resulting byte array, which is why both the encrypt and the decrypt side end with it.
cards.example:
try {
    javax.crypto.Cipher c = javax.crypto.Cipher.getInstance("AES");
    c.init(javax.crypto.Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, javax.crypto.KeyGenerator.getInstance("AES").generateKey());
    byte[] out = c.doFinal("msg".getBytes());   // one-part encrypt/decrypt, or finishes multi-part work
} catch (Exception e) { }

cards.front: Since JDK 19, what is the default RSA key size?
cards.extra: RSASSA-PSS and DH moved too. Small keys are now considered weak against modern factoring capacity.
cards.example:
import java.security.*;
import java.security.interfaces.RSAKey;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
KeyPair kp = KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("RSA").generateKeyPair();
System.out.println(((RSAKey) kp.getPublic()).getModulus().bitLength());
} }

cards.front: What is a digital signature made from?
cards.back: A hash of the message, encrypted with the sender's private key
cards.extra: The receiver recomputes the digest and verifies with the sender's public key, which proves both origin and integrity.
cards.example:
try {
    java.security.Signature sig = java.security.Signature.getInstance("Ed25519");
    sig.initSign(java.security.KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("Ed25519").generateKeyPair().getPrivate());   // sender's private key
    sig.update("message".getBytes());
    byte[] signature = sig.sign();   // hash signed with that private key
} catch (Exception e) { }

cards.front: Which jcmd subcommand prints a running application's system properties?
cards.extra: Scan the output for a suspicious library name, then examine that library to learn its version.
cards.example:
String cmd = "jcmd <pid> VM.system_properties";   // prints a running app's system properties
System.out.println(cmd);

cards.front: Which jcmd subcommand prints loaded classes hierarchically since JDK 9?
cards.extra: Before JDK 9 the only option was GC.class_histogram, which lists instantiated classes rather than loaded ones.
cards.example:
String cmd = "jcmd <pid> VM.class_hierarchy";   // loaded classes hierarchically, since JDK 9
System.out.println(cmd);

cards.front: Does a class missing from jdeps output mean it can never be loaded?
cards.back: No - plugins via reflection or proxy can load classes not seen statically
cards.extra: jdeps analyzes bytecode references. Frameworks that load by name only appear at runtime.
cards.example:
try {
    Class<?> c = Class.forName("com.example.Plugin");   // dynamic load: absent from static jdeps output
    System.out.println(c.getName());                          // plugins/proxies can load unseen classes
} catch (Exception e) { }

cards.front: Which tool statically analyzes a JAR's package and class dependencies?
cards.extra: Its -p option filters packages, and regex support lets you hunt partial package names such as shaded libraries.
cards.example:
String cmd = "jdeps app.jar";   // static analysis of a JAR's package and class dependencies
System.out.println(cmd);

cards.front: Which two system properties disable JNDI object factories in a Java runtime?
cards.extra: The first blocks all object factories, the second stops deserialization from the LDAP javaSerializedData attribute.
cards.example:
class Ex { static void m() {
System.setProperty("jdk.jndi.object.factoriesFilter", "!*");
System.setProperty("trustSerialData", "false");
System.out.println(System.getProperty("jdk.jndi.object.factoriesFilter"));
} }

cards.front: Which system property applies a serialization filter to incoming object streams?
cards.extra: It limits which classes may be deserialized. On the command line both JNDI patches and unlimited native access can be passed via JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS.
cards.example:
import java.io.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
System.setProperty("jdk.serialFilter", "!*");
ObjectInputFilter f = ObjectInputFilter.Config.createFilter(System.getProperty("jdk.serialFilter"));
System.out.println(f);
} }

cards.front: Which command lists the modules inside a JDK runtime image?
cards.extra: Run it against the custom runtime to verify all required modules are present before shipping.
cards.example:
String command = "java --list-modules";   // lists modules inside a JDK runtime image
System.out.println(command);

cards.front: Which jdeps option produces the module list for jlink --add-modules?
cards.extra: It emits a comma-separated list of modules, plus their transitive dependencies, that you can feed straight to jlink.
cards.example:
String option = "--print-module-deps";   // jdeps output for jlink --add-modules
System.out.println(option);

cards.front: Which runtime option limits the modules an application can observe without building a custom image?
cards.extra: It was introduced with JEP 261 in JDK 9. The API a module no longer exposes disappears, so code that relies on it breaks.
cards.example:
String option = "--limit-modules";   // limits observable modules without building a custom image
System.out.println(option);

cards.front: Since which JDK release does jdeps exist for static dependency analysis?
cards.extra: Before that there was no supported JDK tool for package-level dependency analysis of a JAR.
cards.example:
int since = 8;   // jdeps has done static dependency analysis since JDK 8
System.out.println("JDK " + since);

cards.front: What three guarantees does a digital signature provide?
cards.extra: It proves who wrote the message, that it was not altered in transit, and that the author cannot deny having sent it.
cards.example:
String[] guarantees = {"Authenticity", "Integrity", "Non-repudiation"};   // all three come from a digital signature
System.out.println(String.join(", ", guarantees));

cards.front: Which algorithm is used in the article's digital signature example?
cards.back: Ed25519 - an elliptic curve signature using EdDSA over Curve25519
cards.extra: You obtain a Signature instance with Signature.getInstance("Ed25519") and initialize it with the private key to sign.
cards.example:
try {
    java.security.Signature s = java.security.Signature.getInstance("Ed25519");   // EdDSA over Curve25519
    System.out.println(s.getAlgorithm());
} catch (Exception e) { }

cards.front: Which method verifies a signature in Java?
cards.extra: You initialize the Signature instance with the signer's public key and feed it the message before calling verify.
cards.example:
try {
    java.security.Signature signature = java.security.Signature.getInstance("Ed25519");
    signature.initVerify(java.security.KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("Ed25519").generateKeyPair().getPublic());
    boolean ok = signature.verify(new byte[]{1});   // verify(byte[]) returns a boolean
    System.out.println(ok);
} catch (Exception e) { }

cards.front: What does the certification authority (CA) vouch for in a digital certificate?
cards.back: The link between a public key and the identity that owns it
cards.extra: A CA signs the certificate, so a trusting party can rely on the binding without out-of-band key exchange.
cards.example:
String vouch = "public key -> identity that owns it";   // what the CA vouches for in a certificate
System.out.println(vouch);

cards.front: What fields does a digital certificate contain?
cards.back: Serial number, validity dates, subject name and public key, issuer's signature
cards.extra: The public key inside the certificate is what you use to verify the holder's signatures or encrypt to them.
cards.example:
java.security.cert.X509Certificate cert = null;   // serial number, validity dates, subject name and public key
System.out.println(cert.getIssuerX500Principal());   // issuer's signature is also inside it

cards.front: What is a self-signed certificate?
cards.back: One issued by the server that hosts it, not by a known CA
cards.extra: Browsers treat it as untrusted by default because nothing verifies the issuer's own identity.
cards.example:
boolean selfSigned = true;   // issued by the server hosting it, not by a known CA
System.out.println(selfSigned);

cards.front: Which standard defines the format of digital certificates?
cards.extra: Digital signatures use the Digital Signature Standard (DSS) instead. The two are different standards with different jobs.
cards.example:
String standard = "X.509";   // standard defining the format of digital certificates
System.out.println(standard);

cards.front: Which class offers standard access to all the attributes of an X.509 certificate?
cards.extra: The parent java.security.cert.Certificate is the format-agnostic abstraction; X509Certificate adds the fields.
cards.example:
Class<?> c = java.security.cert.X509Certificate.class;   // standard access to all X.509 certificate attributes
System.out.println(c.getName());

cards.front: How do you compute a certificate's thumbprint?
cards.back: Run MessageDigest over the certificate's encoded form
cards.extra: The digest is the unique identifier you compare against a stored fingerprint to confirm you have the right certificate.
cards.example:
try {
    java.security.cert.X509Certificate cert = null;
    byte[] thumbprint = java.security.MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256").digest(cert.getEncoded());   // hash of the encoded form
} catch (Exception e) { }

cards.front: Which two classes validate an X.509 certificate chain?
cards.extra: The trust anchor is the root you already trust, and the validator checks each link from there to the presented certificate.
cards.example:
Class<?>[] validators = {java.security.cert.TrustAnchor.class, java.security.cert.CertPathValidator.class};
System.out.println(validators.length);   // the two classes that validate an X.509 chain

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::04 Cryptography

cards.front: Which JDK release introduced the four JFR security events?
cards.extra: They are disabled by default in the default.jfc and profile.jfc configurations, so you have to enable them explicitly.
cards.example:
int release = 12;   // JDK that introduced the four JFR security events
System.out.println("JDK " + release);

cards.front: Which JFR event records calls to Security.setProperty()?
cards.extra: Paired with the initial-value event, it shows the starting security configuration and every later change.
cards.example:
String event = "jdk.SecurityPropertyModification";   // records Security.setProperty() calls
System.out.println(event);

cards.front: Which JFR event captures the TLS version and cipher suite negotiated on each handshake?
cards.extra: Its fields include peer host, peer port, negotiated protocol and cipher, and the peer certificate id.
cards.example:
String event = "jdk.TLSHandshake";   // TLS version and cipher suite negotiated on each handshake
System.out.println(event);

cards.front: Which JFR event records details of successfully validated X.509 certificates?
cards.extra: jdk.X509Certificate captures every certificate generated by the security libraries, validated or not.
cards.example:
String event = "jdk.X509Validation";   // details of successfully validated X.509 certificates
System.out.println(event);

cards.front: Which system property prints TLS handshake detail, including the selected protocol version?
cards.extra: The output includes a line such as "selected version": [TLSv1.3], which tells you exactly what was negotiated.
cards.example:
String property = "-Djavax.net.debug=ssl:handshake";   // handshake detail incl. selected protocol version
System.out.println(property);

cards.front: Which JFR event shows initial JDK security property values?
cards.extra: It is enabled by default, unlike the modification event, so a recording always has the baseline to compare against.
cards.example:
String event = "jdk.InitialSecurityProperty";   // initial JDK security property values, added in JDK 20
System.out.println(event);

cards.front: Which one-word system property prints initial security properties to standard error?
cards.extra: It is a quick alternative to a JFR recording when you only need the startup snapshot.
cards.example:
String property = "-Djava.security.debug=properties";   // prints initial security properties to stderr
System.out.println(property);

cards.front: Which JFR event tracks how often service provider implementations are invoked?
cards.extra: It counts service provider calls, which reveals which crypto implementations actually do the work at runtime.
cards.example:
String event = "jdk.SecurityProviderService";   // counts service provider implementation invocations
System.out.println(event);

cards.front: Which fields identify an X.509 certificate for expiry monitoring?
cards.back: Its validity period, along with subject, issuer and serial number
cards.extra: An expired certificate breaks connections from a specific date, so the not-after value is the field worth alerting on.
cards.example:
String fields = "validity period, subject, issuer, serial number";   // identify a certificate for expiry monitoring
System.out.println(fields);

cards.front: Since which JDK release can JFR events be streamed programmatically over the network instead of only via JMC?
cards.back: JDK 14 (JEP 349) — no flight recording file is needed
cards.extra: An MBeanServerConnection lets you pull recorded events as they occur, which enables custom monitoring dashboards.
cards.example:
import jdk.jfr.consumer.*;
class Ex { static void m() {
String release = "JDK 16";
try (RecordingStream s = new RecordingStream()) { s.enable("jdk.JavaMonitorWait"); s.onEvent(e -> System.out.println(release)); s.startAsync(); }
} }

cards.front: Which default TLS versions do recent JDKs negotiate?
cards.extra: Which one a particular socket uses depends on both peers, so measure rather than assume.
cards.example:
import javax.net.ssl.*;
import java.util.Arrays;
class Ex { static void m() throws Exception {
SSLContext ctx = SSLContext.getDefault();
System.out.println(Arrays.toString(ctx.getDefaultSSLParameters().getProtocols()));
} }

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::05 Date and Time

cards.front: Which class represents a date with no time and no time zone?
cards.extra: It holds a year, month and day in the ISO calendar, which suits things like birthdays that are the same date everywhere.
cards.example:
java.time.LocalDate d = java.time.LocalDate.of(2013, 8, 20);
System.out.println(d);
System.out.println(java.time.LocalDateTime.of(d, java.time.LocalTime.NOON));

cards.front: Which class represents a month of a specific year?
cards.extra: lengthOfMonth() answers how many days it has, which correctly handles February in leap years.
cards.example:
java.time.YearMonth month = java.time.YearMonth.of(2024, java.time.Month.FEBRUARY);
System.out.println(month); // 2024-02
System.out.println(month.lengthOfMonth()); // 29

cards.front: Which class represents a month and day with no year, such as New Year's Day?
cards.extra: isValidYear() then asks whether that day exists in a given year, so February 29 is valid in 2012 but not 2010.
cards.example:
java.time.MonthDay newYear = java.time.MonthDay.of(1, 1);   // month and day, no year
System.out.println(newYear);

cards.front: Which class represents a year alone?
cards.extra: isLeap() reports leap-year status, so Year.of(2012).isLeap() is true.
cards.example:
java.time.Year year = java.time.Year.of(2024);
System.out.println(year.isLeap()); // true
System.out.println(year.length()); // 366

cards.front: Which method on LocalDate returns the day of the week the date falls on?
cards.extra: It returns a DayOfWeek enum constant such as MONDAY, not a number, which keeps the code readable.
cards.example:
java.time.LocalDate date = java.time.LocalDate.of(2024, 1, 1);
System.out.println(date.getDayOfWeek());   // day of the week this date falls on

cards.front: How do you find the first Wednesday after a given date?
cards.extra: A TemporalAdjuster returns an adjusted temporal value, and with() applies it to produce a new immutable date.
cards.example:
java.time.LocalDate date = java.time.LocalDate.of(2024, 1, 1);
java.time.LocalDate wed = date.with(java.time.temporal.TemporalAdjusters.next(java.time.DayOfWeek.WEDNESDAY));
System.out.println(wed); // 2024-01-03

cards.front: How many date-only classes does the Date-Time API provide, and which?
cards.extra: Each models a different precision of date information, so you pick the narrowest one that fits the fact you store.
cards.example:
java.time.LocalDate d = java.time.LocalDate.of(2013, 8, 20);
java.time.YearMonth ym = java.time.YearMonth.of(2013, 8);
java.time.MonthDay md = java.time.MonthDay.of(8, 20);
java.time.Year y = java.time.Year.of(2013);
System.out.println(d + " " + ym + " " + md + " " + y);

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::05 Date and Time

cards.front: What integer values do DayOfWeek constants have?
cards.extra: The numbering follows the ISO standard, which starts the week on Monday rather than Sunday.
cards.example:
System.out.println(java.time.DayOfWeek.MONDAY.getValue()); // 1
System.out.println(java.time.DayOfWeek.SUNDAY.getValue()); // 7

cards.front: What integer values do Month constants have?
cards.extra: This matches the ISO month range, and unlike legacy Calendar it is 1-based.
cards.example:
System.out.println(java.time.Month.JANUARY.getValue()); // 1
System.out.println(java.time.Month.DECEMBER.getValue()); // 12

cards.front: Which method gives a localized name for a day or month?
cards.extra: TextStyle chooses FULL, SHORT or NARROW. STANDALONE variants exist where a language names the month differently in isolation.
cards.example:
java.time.DayOfWeek day = java.time.DayOfWeek.MONDAY;
System.out.println(day.getDisplayName(java.time.format.TextStyle.FULL, java.util.Locale.FRENCH));
System.out.println(java.time.Month.JANUARY.getDisplayName(java.time.format.TextStyle.SHORT, java.util.Locale.ENGLISH));

cards.front: What does Month.FEBRUARY.maxLength() return?
cards.extra: It is the most days the month can ever have, so leap years are included. YearMonth.lengthOfMonth() gives the value for a specific year.
cards.example:
java.time.Month m = java.time.Month.FEBRUARY;
System.out.println(m.maxLength());

cards.front: What does DayOfWeek.MONDAY.plus(3) return?
cards.extra: Enum constants support temporal arithmetic directly, wrapping around at the end of the week.
cards.example:
java.time.DayOfWeek day = java.time.DayOfWeek.MONDAY;
java.time.DayOfWeek later = day.plus(3);
System.out.println(later);
