cards.front: What does an Instant represent?
cards.back: A single point on the timeline, measured from the epoch with nanosecond precision
cards.extra: The epoch is 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z. Instant is designed for machine timestamps, not for human dates.
cards.example:
java.time.Instant instant = java.time.Instant.ofEpochSecond(0, 123456789);
System.out.println(instant); // 1970-01-01T00:00:00.123456789Z

cards.front: What count does an Instant store internally?
cards.extra: An instant before the epoch has a negative value. MIN and MAX bound the representable range.
cards.example:
java.time.Instant i = java.time.Instant.parse("1970-01-01T00:00:01.000000123Z");
System.out.println(i.getEpochSecond() + " " + i.getNano());

cards.front: Which format does Instant.toString() produce?
cards.extra: The trailing Z marks UTC. Switching between this text form and other classes goes through the same standard.
cards.example:
java.time.Instant instant = java.time.Instant.parse("2013-08-20T15:16:26.355Z");
System.out.println(instant.toString()); // 2013-08-20T15:16:26.355Z

cards.front: Can an Instant be expressed in years, months or days?
cards.back: No - it only knows seconds and nanoseconds
cards.extra: Those units depend on a time zone. Bind the Instant to a ZonedDateTime or LocalDateTime first to use them.
cards.example:
java.time.Instant i = java.time.Instant.parse("2024-01-01T00:00:00Z");
System.out.println(i.getEpochSecond() + " " + i.getNano());
// ChronoUnit.MONTHS.between(i, i) throws UnsupportedTemporalTypeException

cards.front: To do year or month arithmetic with an Instant, what must you do first?
cards.back: Convert it with a time zone to a ZonedDateTime or LocalDateTime
cards.extra: LocalDateTime.ofInstant(instant, zone) is the conversion, and then years, months and days become meaningful.
cards.example:
java.time.Instant i = java.time.Instant.parse("2024-01-01T00:00:00Z");
java.time.LocalDateTime dt = java.time.LocalDateTime.ofInstant(i, java.time.ZoneId.of("Asia/Tokyo"));
System.out.println(dt.plusMonths(1).plusYears(1));

cards.front: Which method measures the elapsed time between two Instant objects?
cards.extra: isAfter() and isBefore() just compare. until() returns an amount in the chosen unit, such as seconds or hours.
cards.example:
java.time.Instant a = java.time.Instant.parse("2024-01-01T00:00:00Z");
java.time.Instant b = java.time.Instant.parse("2024-01-01T00:00:05Z");
System.out.println(a.until(b, java.time.temporal.ChronoUnit.SECONDS));

cards.front: Which class can be converted to an Instant without extra information?
cards.extra: ZonedDateTime and OffsetDateTime map to an exact moment; a LocalDateTime is ambiguous without an offset.
cards.example:
java.time.Instant a = java.time.ZonedDateTime.now().toInstant();
java.time.Instant b = java.time.OffsetDateTime.now().toInstant();
// java.time.LocalDateTime.now().toInstant() does not exist
System.out.println(a + " " + b);

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::05 Date and Time

cards.front: Which calendar system does the Date-Time API use by default?
cards.back: The ISO-8601 calendar, based on the Gregorian calendar
cards.extra: Alternative systems such as Hijrah or Thai Buddhist live in java.time.chrono, and you may define your own.
cards.example:
java.time.chrono.Chronology iso = java.time.chrono.IsoChronology.INSTANCE;
java.time.LocalDate date = java.time.LocalDate.of(2024, 1, 2);
System.out.println(date.getChronology() == iso); // true by default

cards.front: What are the four design principles of the Date-Time API?
cards.extra: Immutable is what makes the whole API thread-safe: every modification returns a new object instead of mutating one.
cards.example:
java.time.LocalDate d = java.time.LocalDate.of(2024, 1, 1);
System.out.println(d.plusDays(1).withMonth(2)); // clear and fluent: a new value
System.out.println(d); // immutable: original unchanged
java.time.LocalDate first = d.with(java.time.temporal.TemporalAdjusters.firstDayOfMonth()); // extensible

cards.front: Why is the Date-Time API thread-safe?
cards.back: Its classes are immutable, so no shared state can be mutated
cards.extra: This is the direct answer to the legacy Calendar and SimpleDateFormat problems, where shared mutable state caused data races.
cards.example:
java.time.LocalDate d = java.time.LocalDate.of(2024, 1, 1);
java.time.LocalDate next = d.plusDays(1);
System.out.println(d + " " + next); // original d is unchanged

cards.front: Which method prefix creates an instance by validating its input parameters?
cards.extra: It checks that the fields form a valid date. from() converts another type instead, and parse() reads text.
cards.example:
java.time.LocalDate d = java.time.LocalDate.of(2024, 2, 29);
System.out.println(d);
// java.time.LocalDate.of(2023, 2, 29) throws java.time.DateTimeException

cards.front: Which method prefix converts another object to the target type, possibly losing information?
cards.extra: For example LocalDate.from(temporal) extracts the date part. Information beyond the target type's precision is discarded.
cards.example:
java.time.LocalDateTime ldt = java.time.LocalDateTime.of(2013, 8, 20, 12, 30);
java.time.LocalDate d = java.time.LocalDate.from(ldt);
System.out.println(d);

cards.front: Which method prefix is the immutable equivalent of a setter?
cards.extra: It returns a copy with one element changed. plus() and minus() are the same idea for adding or subtracting time.
cards.example:
java.time.LocalDate d = java.time.LocalDate.of(2013, 8, 20);
java.time.LocalDate next = d.with(java.time.temporal.ChronoField.DAY_OF_MONTH, 21);
System.out.println(d + " -> " + next);

cards.front: Which method prefix combines one temporal object with another?
cards.extra: A LocalDate at a time zone becomes a ZonedDateTime, and at a LocalTime becomes a LocalDateTime.
cards.example:
java.time.LocalDate date = java.time.LocalDate.of(2013, 8, 20);
java.time.LocalDateTime dt = date.atTime(12, 30);
System.out.println(dt);

cards.front: What happens when you pass null to a Date-Time method parameter?
cards.extra: Nulls are rejected rather than silently accepted, which is part of the clear design and keeps fluent chains safe.
cards.example:
try {
    java.time.LocalDate.from(null);
} catch (NullPointerException e) {
    System.out.println("NullPointerException");
}

cards.front: Which package holds the formatters and parsers for dates and times?
cards.extra: Mobile java.time.zone instead handles zone rules and offsets. java.time.temporal holds fields, units, adjusters and queries.
cards.example:
java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter f = java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter.ISO_LOCAL_DATE;
System.out.println(f.format(java.time.LocalDate.of(2024, 1, 2)));

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::05 Date and Time

cards.front: Which method converts a legacy Date to an Instant?
cards.extra: Date.from(Instant) goes the other way. Both classes model an instant independent of any time zone.
cards.example:
java.util.Date date = java.util.Date.from(java.time.Instant.parse("2024-01-01T00:00:00Z"));
java.time.Instant i = date.toInstant();
System.out.println(i);

cards.front: Which method converts a Calendar to a ZonedDateTime?
cards.extra: Calendar has no direct toZonedDateTime(), so the conversion goes through Instant plus an explicit zone.
cards.example:
java.util.Calendar calendar = java.util.Calendar.getInstance();
java.time.ZoneId zone = java.time.ZoneId.systemDefault();
java.time.ZonedDateTime zdt = calendar.toInstant().atZone(zone);
System.out.println(zdt);

cards.front: Which method converts a TimeZone to a ZoneId?
cards.extra: TimeZone could not express the rules the Date-Time API needs, while ZoneId carries them.
cards.example:
java.util.TimeZone tz = java.util.TimeZone.getTimeZone("Asia/Tokyo");
java.time.ZoneId z = tz.toZoneId();
System.out.println(z.getId());

cards.front: Why could legacy Calendar objects not be shared between threads?
cards.extra: Date-Time classes replaced them with immutable, thread-safe value objects that never change after creation.
cards.example:
java.util.Calendar c = java.util.Calendar.getInstance();
c.set(java.util.Calendar.YEAR, 2024);
// mutable: another thread could set() the same Calendar object
System.out.println(c.get(java.util.Calendar.YEAR));

cards.front: What replaces a legacy GregorianCalendar with the time set to 00:00 to hold a date?
cards.extra: Even midnight is unreliable: in some countries a daylight-saving transition skips it once a year.
cards.example:
java.util.GregorianCalendar legacy = new java.util.GregorianCalendar(2024, java.util.Calendar.JANUARY, 2);
java.time.LocalDate modern = java.time.LocalDate.of(2024, 1, 2);
System.out.println(modern);

cards.front: Which Date-Time class replaces a legacy GregorianCalendar used for both date and zone?
cards.extra: GregorianCalendar.from(zoned) and toZonedDateTime() bridge the two as the migration route.
cards.example:
java.util.GregorianCalendar legacy = new java.util.GregorianCalendar(java.util.TimeZone.getTimeZone("Europe/Paris"));
java.time.ZonedDateTime modern = java.time.ZonedDateTime.ofInstant(legacy.toInstant(), legacy.getTimeZone().toZoneId());
System.out.println(modern);

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::05 Date and Time

cards.front: Which class represents a time of day with no date and no zone?
cards.extra: It stores hour, minute, second and nanosecond, which suits opening hours or a movie schedule.
cards.example:
java.time.LocalTime t = java.time.LocalTime.of(12, 30, 15, 123456789);
System.out.println(t);
System.out.println(t.getHour() + ":" + t.getMinute());

cards.front: Does LocalTime know about daylight saving time?
cards.back: No - it stores no zone or DST information
cards.extra: DST is defined relative to a zone, so a zone-independent time cannot know whether a given hour exists or repeats.
cards.example:
java.time.LocalTime t = java.time.LocalTime.of(12, 30);
System.out.println(t);
System.out.println(t.atOffset(java.time.ZoneOffset.ofHours(9)));

cards.front: Which class combines a date and a time without a zone?
cards.extra: It is effectively LocalDate plus LocalTime. To pin it to a moment you need a ZonedDateTime or OffsetDateTime.
cards.example:
java.time.LocalDateTime dt = java.time.LocalDateTime.of(2013, 8, 20, 12, 30);
System.out.println(dt);
System.out.println(dt.toLocalDate() + " " + dt.toLocalTime());

cards.front: Which class do you need to attach a time zone to a date and time?
cards.extra: LocalDateTime deliberately has no zone, so it names a wall-clock reading rather than an instant on the timeline.
cards.example:
java.time.LocalDateTime local = java.time.LocalDateTime.of(2024, 1, 2, 3, 4);
java.time.ZonedDateTime zoned = local.atZone(java.time.ZoneId.of("Europe/Paris"));
java.time.OffsetDateTime offset = local.atOffset(java.time.ZoneOffset.ofHours(2));
System.out.println(zoned + " " + offset);

cards.front: Which method gives the current date and time as a LocalDateTime?
cards.extra: Every temporal class offers now(), which captures the current moment in the fields that class models, discarding the rest.
cards.example:
java.time.LocalDateTime now = java.time.LocalDateTime.now();
System.out.println(now);

cards.front: How do you add hours or days to a LocalDateTime?
cards.extra: The minus equivalents subtract, and every call returns a new instance rather than mutating the receiver.
cards.example:
java.time.LocalDateTime t = java.time.LocalDateTime.of(2024, 1, 10, 12, 0);
System.out.println(t.plusHours(2));
System.out.println(t.plusDays(1).plusMonths(1));

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::05 Date and Time

cards.front: Which package holds the predefined non-ISO chronologies?
cards.extra: It offers Japanese, Hijrah, Minguo and Thai Buddhist among others, and lets you implement your own.
cards.example:
java.time.chrono.JapaneseDate j = java.time.chrono.JapaneseDate.now();
java.time.chrono.HijrahDate h = java.time.chrono.HijrahDate.now();
java.time.chrono.MinguoDate m = java.time.chrono.MinguoDate.now();
java.time.chrono.ThaiBuddhistDate t = java.time.chrono.ThaiBuddhistDate.now();
System.out.println(j.getClass().getPackage().getName() + " " + h + " " + m + " " + t);

cards.front: Which static method converts an ISO date to another chronology such as JapaneseDate?
cards.extra: Supply a LocalDateTime, LocalDate or similar. It throws DateTimeException when the input cannot form a valid date.
cards.example:
java.time.LocalDate iso = java.time.LocalDate.of(2013, 8, 20);
java.time.chrono.JapaneseDate jd = java.time.chrono.JapaneseDate.from(iso);
System.out.println(jd);

cards.front: Which method converts a non-ISO date back to an ISO LocalDate?
cards.extra: It throws DateTimeException if the given date cannot be converted, so guard the call when input is untrusted.
cards.example:
java.time.LocalDate iso = java.time.LocalDate.of(2013, 8, 20);
java.time.chrono.JapaneseDate jd = java.time.chrono.JapaneseDate.from(iso);
System.out.println(java.time.LocalDate.from(jd));

cards.front: Which method would a non-ISO date use to report its chronology object?
cards.extra: The returned Chronology also provides ISO conversion methods, which is how you get a ISO weekend or field semantics.
cards.example:
java.time.chrono.ChronoLocalDate date = java.time.chrono.JapaneseDate.now();
java.time.chrono.Chronology chronology = date.getChronology();
System.out.println(chronology);

cards.front: What does DateTimeFormatterBuilder add over a plain DateTimeFormatter?
cards.back: You can assemble a format step by step, including for a non-ISO chronology
cards.extra: it to build the string for a converted date, so a chronology-specific rendering becomes possible.
cards.example:
java.time.format.DateTimeFormatterBuilder b = new java.time.format.DateTimeFormatterBuilder();
b.appendValue(java.time.temporal.ChronoField.DAY_OF_MONTH);
java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter f = b.toFormatter();
System.out.println(f.format(java.time.chrono.JapaneseDate.now()));

cards.front: Which exception do the non-ISO conversions throw when a date cannot be converted?
cards.extra: Both directions throw it: converting to a chronology and converting back to LocalDate with from().
cards.example:
try {
    java.time.chrono.JapaneseDate.from(java.time.LocalTime.NOON);
} catch (java.time.DateTimeException e) {
    System.out.println(e.getClass().getSimpleName());
}

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::05 Date and Time

cards.front: Which class both parses strings into dates and formats dates into strings?
cards.extra: You choose a predefined formatter or a pattern, then pass it to parse() or format() on the temporal object.
cards.example:
java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter f = java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter.ISO_LOCAL_DATE;
String text = f.format(java.time.LocalDate.of(2013, 8, 20));
System.out.println(text + " -> " + java.time.LocalDate.parse(text, f));

cards.front: Which exception should parse code catch?
cards.extra: Formatting throws DateTimeException instead, so the catch clause depends on which direction you are going.
cards.example:
try {
    java.time.LocalDate.parse("not-a-date", java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter.ISO_LOCAL_DATE);
} catch (java.time.format.DateTimeParseException e) {
    System.out.println(e.getClass().getSimpleName());
}

cards.front: Is DateTimeFormatter immutable and thread-safe?
cards.back: Yes, so it should be stored in a static constant
cards.extra: That is a major improvement over SimpleDateFormat, which was mutable and unsafe to share between threads.
cards.example:
class Ex {
    static final java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter F = java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter.ISO_LOCAL_DATE;
    static void m() {
        System.out.println(F.format(java.time.LocalDate.of(2013, 8, 20)));
    }
}

cards.front: Which predefined formatter produces 19590709 for July 9, 1959?
cards.extra: The one-argument parse() on LocalDate uses ISO_LOCAL_DATE instead, which takes hyphenated input.
cards.example:
java.time.LocalDate d = java.time.LocalDate.of(1959, 7, 9);
String s = java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter.BASIC_ISO_DATE.format(d);
System.out.println(s);

cards.front: In a date pattern such as MMM d yyyy, what does d mean versus dd?
cards.back: d accepts one or two digits; dd requires exactly two, zero-padded
cards.extra: So MMM dd yyyy needs "Jun 03 2003", while MMM d yyyy accepts "Jun 3 2003".
cards.example:
java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter one = java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("MMM d yyyy");
java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter two = java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("MMM dd yyyy");
System.out.println(java.time.LocalDate.parse("Jun 3 2003", one));
System.out.println(java.time.LocalDate.parse("Jun 03 2003", two));

cards.front: Which pattern letter sequence represents the hour in 12-hour form, as in the article's example?
cards.back: hh, usually paired with a for the AM/PM marker
cards.extra: hh for two-digit 12-hour time and a to add the a.m. or p.m. text.
cards.example:
java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter f = java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("hh a");
System.out.println(f.format(java.time.LocalTime.of(15, 16))); // 03 PM

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::05 Date and Time

cards.front: What does a Duration measure?
cards.back: A fixed length of time in seconds and nanoseconds
cards.extra: It suits machine time such as Instant math. A one-day Duration is always exactly 24 hours.
cards.example:
java.time.Duration d = java.time.Duration.ofSeconds(90, 123);
System.out.println(d.getSeconds() + " " + d.getNano());
System.out.println(d);

cards.front: What does a Period measure?
cards.back: A date-based amount expressed as years, months and days
cards.extra: Because it is date-based, a one-day Period added to a ZonedDateTime can be 23 or 25 hours across a DST change.
cards.example:
java.time.Period p = java.time.Period.of(1, 2, 3);
System.out.println(p.getYears() + " " + p.getMonths() + " " + p.getDays());
System.out.println(java.time.LocalDate.of(2024, 1, 31).plus(p));

cards.front: What is the key difference between a one day Duration and a one day Period?
cards.back: The Duration is exactly 24 hours; the Period can be 23 or 25 hours in a zone
cards.extra: The Duration is an absolute time amount, while the Period is measured in calendar units whose real length depends on the date.
cards.example:
java.time.ZoneId zone = java.time.ZoneId.of("Europe/Paris");
java.time.ZonedDateTime start = java.time.ZonedDateTime.of(2024, 3, 31, 0, 0, 0, 0, zone);
java.time.ZonedDateTime end = start.plusDays(1);
System.out.println(java.time.Duration.ofDays(1) + " " + java.time.Period.ofDays(1));
System.out.println(java.time.temporal.ChronoUnit.HOURS.between(start, end)); // 23 in the zone

cards.front: Can a Duration be negative?
cards.back: Yes, if the end point is before the start point
cards.extra: ChronoUnit.between() behaves the same way, returning a negative amount for a reversed pair.
cards.example:
java.time.Instant end = java.time.Instant.parse("2024-01-01T00:00:00Z");
java.time.Instant start = java.time.Instant.parse("2024-01-02T00:00:00Z");
System.out.println(java.time.Duration.between(start, end).isNegative());

cards.front: Is a Duration tied to a time zone?
cards.back: No - it tracks neither zone nor daylight saving time
cards.extra: That independence is why Duration is the correct type for elapsed-time measurement and for timeouts.
cards.example:
java.time.Duration d = java.time.Duration.ofHours(24);
System.out.println(d.getSeconds());
System.out.println(d);

cards.front: Which method measures the amount of time between two temporal objects in a single unit?
cards.extra: It works with any temporal type but reports only one unit, so a total in days or in milliseconds is a single call.
cards.example:
java.time.LocalDate start = java.time.LocalDate.of(2024, 1, 1);
java.time.LocalDate end = java.time.LocalDate.of(2024, 1, 11);
System.out.println(java.time.temporal.ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(start, end)); // 10

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::05 Date and Time

cards.front: What are the two basic ways to represent time in the Date-Time API?
cards.back: Human time (year, month, day) and machine time (a point on a timeline)
cards.extra: Pick human time for local schedules and machine time for timestamps and elapsed measurement.
cards.example:
java.time.LocalDate human = java.time.LocalDate.of(2024, 1, 2);
long machine = java.time.Instant.parse("2024-01-02T00:00:00Z").toEpochMilli();
System.out.println(human + " " + machine);

cards.front: Which class represents human time as year, month and day only?
cards.extra: Its toString() prints 2013-08-20. A birthday is the classic case, since the same date applies worldwide.
cards.example:
java.time.LocalDate d = java.time.LocalDate.of(2013, 8, 20);
System.out.println(d);
System.out.println(d.getYear() + "-" + d.getMonthValue() + "-" + d.getDayOfMonth());

cards.front: Which class stores a full date and time together with a zone ID and offset?
cards.extra: Its toString() shows both, such as 2013-08-21T00:16:26.941+09:00[Asia/Tokyo].
cards.example:
java.time.ZonedDateTime zdt = java.time.ZonedDateTime.of(2024, 1, 2, 3, 4, 0, 0, java.time.ZoneId.of("Europe/Paris"));
System.out.println(zdt.getZone()); // Europe/Paris
System.out.println(zdt.getOffset()); // +01:00

cards.front: Which class stores an offset but no zone ID?
cards.back: OffsetDateTime, or OffsetTime when the date is not needed
cards.extra: Offsets come from network and XML formats, while zone IDs are needed to apply daylight-saving rules.
cards.example:
java.time.OffsetDateTime odt = java.time.OffsetDateTime.of(2013, 8, 20, 12, 30, 0, 0, java.time.ZoneOffset.ofHours(9));
System.out.println(odt.getOffset());
java.time.OffsetTime ot = java.time.OffsetTime.of(12, 30, 0, 0, java.time.ZoneOffset.ofHours(9));
System.out.println(ot);

cards.front: What does Duration's toString() produce for 20 hours?
cards.extra: The ISO-8601 duration form puts a T between the date part and the time part, so hours alone need PT.
cards.example:
java.time.Duration d = java.time.Duration.ofHours(20);
System.out.println(d.toString()); // PT20H

cards.front: What does Period.P10D's toString() produce?
cards.extra: Date-based amounts need no T separator, so ten days is simply P10D.
cards.example:
java.time.Period p = java.time.Period.ofDays(10);
System.out.println(p.toString()); // P10D

cards.front: What does MonthDay's toString() print for August 20?
cards.extra: The two hyphens stand in for the year a MonthDay does not carry. Its sibling YearMonth prints with the year first, as in 2013-08.
cards.example:
java.time.MonthDay md = java.time.MonthDay.of(java.time.Month.AUGUST, 20);
System.out.println(md);

cards.front: Which interface supplies the read-only framework for date-time classes?
cards.extra: Temporal adds the write side, so it is a TemporalAccessor plus arithmetic. LocalDate, Instant and ZonedDateTime implement Temporal.
cards.example:
java.time.temporal.TemporalAccessor t = java.time.LocalDate.of(2013, 8, 20);
System.out.println(t.isSupported(java.time.temporal.ChronoField.DAY_OF_MONTH));
System.out.println(t.get(java.time.temporal.ChronoField.DAY_OF_MONTH));

cards.front: Which concrete class implements TemporalField and provides constants such as DAY_OF_WEEK?
cards.extra: A field is a component of a date such as month-of-year. Its unit is described by a TemporalUnit such as ChronoUnit.MONTHS.
cards.example:
java.time.temporal.TemporalField field = java.time.temporal.ChronoField.DAY_OF_WEEK;
System.out.println(java.time.LocalDate.of(2024, 1, 1).get(field)); // 1 (Monday)

cards.front: How do you ask whether a temporal object supports a field?
cards.extra: For example LocalDate.isSupported(ChronoField.CLOCK_HOUR_OF_DAY) is false, since a date has no clock.
cards.example:
java.time.temporal.Temporal temporal = java.time.LocalDate.of(2024, 1, 1);
System.out.println(temporal.isSupported(java.time.temporal.ChronoField.DAY_OF_MONTH)); // true
System.out.println(temporal.isSupported(java.time.temporal.ChronoField.HOUR_OF_DAY)); // false

cards.front: Which interface turns a temporal into a new value, typically used through with?
cards.extra: Its adjustInto(Temporal) returns an adjusted value, and with() is the standard way to apply it.
cards.example:
java.time.temporal.TemporalAdjuster adjuster = java.time.temporal.TemporalAdjusters.firstDayOfMonth();
java.time.LocalDate d = java.time.LocalDate.of(2024, 5, 15).with(adjuster);
System.out.println(d); // 2024-05-01

cards.front: Which class holds predefined adjusters like first day of month?
cards.extra: Its methods are static, so a static import gives you names like firstDayOfMonth() and lastInMonth(DayOfWeek).
cards.example:
java.time.LocalDate d = java.time.LocalDate.of(2024, 5, 15);
System.out.println(d.with(java.time.temporal.TemporalAdjusters.firstDayOfMonth())); // 2024-05-01
System.out.println(d.with(java.time.temporal.TemporalAdjusters.lastDayOfMonth())); // 2024-05-31

cards.front: Which interface is implemented to build a custom query of a temporal object?
cards.extra: Its queryFrom(TemporalAccessor) method returns the extracted answer, and query() runs a query against a temporal.
cards.example:
java.time.temporal.TemporalQuery query = t -> java.time.LocalDate.from(t);
System.out.println(java.time.LocalDateTime.of(2024, 1, 2, 3, 4).query(query));

cards.front: Which enum provides standard units from nanoseconds to millennia?
cards.extra: It implements TemporalUnit, and ChronoField values are built from combinations of them.
cards.example:
java.time.temporal.ChronoUnit n = java.time.temporal.ChronoUnit.NANOS;
java.time.temporal.ChronoUnit m = java.time.temporal.ChronoUnit.MILLENNIA;
System.out.println(n + " " + m + " " + java.time.LocalDate.of(2024, 1, 1).plus(1, m));

cards.front: Which class defines ISO-specific fields that ChronoField does not?
cards.extra: It covers things like week-of-week-based-year and quarter-of-year, which only make sense on the ISO calendar.
cards.example:
java.time.LocalDate d = java.time.LocalDate.of(2013, 8, 20);
System.out.println(d.get(java.time.temporal.IsoFields.QUARTER_OF_YEAR));
System.out.println(d.get(java.time.temporal.IsoFields.WEEK_OF_WEEK_BASED_YEAR));

cards.front: What format does a time zone ID usually have?
cards.extra: Each zone also has an offset from Greenwich, plus a set of rules for how that offset changes over time.
cards.example:
java.time.ZoneId z = java.time.ZoneId.of("Asia/Tokyo");
System.out.println(z.getId());
System.out.println(java.time.ZonedDateTime.now(z));

cards.front: Which two classes specify a zone versus a fixed offset?
cards.back: ZoneId for a zone with rules, ZoneOffset for a fixed offset
cards.extra: ZoneId can convert between Instant and LocalDateTime using its region's rules; ZoneOffset can only shift by a fixed amount.
cards.example:
java.time.ZoneId zone = java.time.ZoneId.of("Asia/Tokyo");
java.time.ZoneOffset off = java.time.ZoneOffset.ofHours(9);
System.out.println(zone.getRules());
System.out.println(off);

cards.front: Which class uses ZoneRules to handle daylight-saving gaps and overlaps?
cards.extra: When clocks spring forward an hour, that wall-clock time does not exist; when they fall back it exists twice. ZonedDateTime handles both.
cards.example:
java.time.ZoneId zone = java.time.ZoneId.of("Europe/Paris");
java.time.zone.ZoneRules rules = zone.getRules();
System.out.println(rules.getValidOffsets(java.time.LocalDateTime.of(2024, 3, 31, 2, 30))); // empty gap
System.out.println(java.time.ZonedDateTime.of(2024, 3, 31, 2, 30, 0, 0, zone)); // shifted forward

cards.front: Why can OffsetDateTime not resolve a DST gap or overlap?
cards.back: It has an offset but no zone ID, so it cannot consult the ZoneRules
cards.extra: Without the region's rules it cannot know that 02:30 was skipped or that 01:30 occurred twice that night.
cards.example:
java.time.OffsetDateTime odt = java.time.OffsetDateTime.parse("2024-03-10T02:30:00-05:00");
java.time.ZonedDateTime zdt = java.time.ZonedDateTime.of(2024, 3, 10, 2, 30, 0, 0, java.time.ZoneId.of("America/New_York"));
System.out.println(odt);
System.out.println(zdt);

cards.front: Which class should you use to track a timestamp that records only an absolute offset?
cards.extra: Databases and XML formats often store an offset rather than a region, which makes it the matching type.
cards.example:
java.time.OffsetDateTime stamp = java.time.OffsetDateTime.of(2024, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 0, java.time.ZoneOffset.ofHours(2));
System.out.println(stamp.getOffset()); // +02:00

cards.front: Which method returns the same instant in a different time zone?
cards.extra: Use it for arrival times after a flight. withZoneSameLocal() keeps the wall-clock reading instead.
cards.example:
java.time.ZonedDateTime zdt = java.time.ZonedDateTime.parse("2024-01-01T12:00:00+01:00[Europe/Paris]");
java.time.ZonedDateTime sameInstant = zdt.withZoneSameInstant(java.time.ZoneId.of("Asia/Tokyo"));
System.out.println(zdt + " -> " + sameInstant); // 12:00+01:00 -> 20:00+09:00
